Now when we refer to the Postal Guide we find what these regulations are. We find that the Governor in Council in making the regulations framed under the Act has not attempted in any way to widen the 247
scope of the Act or to give to the officials in the department greater authority than the Act contemplates. On the contrary we find that the order in council on the subject-for I presume the regulations follow7 the order in council-expressly limits the right of the departments to send out matter under frank. The regulation referred to is section 114 and it limits this franking privilege in this way .
All letters and other mail matter sent to the public departments at Ottawa and franked as being of a departmental character.
Now7, Mr. Speaker, I wish to follow that up, and to remind the Postmaster General, because he know7s it much better than I do, what his duty is under the Act in case of continued violation even by one of his colleagues. I read in section 119 of the Act, subsection (e) these words:
Every one who forges, counterfeits or unlawfully imitates, uses or affixes, to or upon any letter or packet, any stamp, signature, initials, or other mark or sign purporting that such letter or packet ought to pass free of postage, or at a lower rate of postage, or that the postage thereon or any part thereof has been pre-paid or ought to be paid or charged to any person or department is guilty of an indictable offence, and liable to imprisonment for life, or for a term not less than five years.
Now, Sir, I do not think that this is a frivolous situation, although I see that the Solicitor General, whose frank is used for this purpose, and also his colleague the Minister of Justice, are much amused at the reading of this section. I can imagine a cause for the gaiety which they exhibit, a cause which has been brought to the notice of the Canadian public on more than one occasion and is now occupying the public mind, that is, that while the Justice Department is the prosecuting department, and the guardian of the administration of the laws of this country, it is also the department which has the power of releasing offenders. Of course, while this Postal Act does say that if any official of that department should be found to have committed this indictable offence and to have rendered himself liable to the punishment prescribed by the Act, yet as an official of the Justice Department he will be very near to the centre of influence over the pardoning power, and therefore it is a matter of pardonable gaiety on the part of the Solicitor General that any member of this House should seriously suggest that he need be in any terror of the law7 in this regard. But. Mr. Speaker, although I am not -an optimist in the matter of impressing this parliament with the seriousness of any offence against law7 or propriety, and I say that with a fresh recollection of recent events in this House, al* though I am not a hopeless optimist in

that respect, I do not think that the hide of parliament is altogether impervious. I do think that parliament has a right to be shocked when we find the Justice Department being used as an agency to beat another department out of the revenue to which it is entitled. That, Mr. Speaker, is my view of the case, and I think it is not a laughing matter on the part of the Minister of Justice or of the Solicitor General.
Now, I would like to emphasize the fact that this matter does not arise casually; it-is not the case of some literary genius connected with the Justice Department writing a pamphlet, writing a circular letter, and for convenience, and in the ordinary course of business, as one might send out his own private correspondence from a department without any violation of the spirit of the law; I wish to point out that this is not a case of that kind at all, that the circular to which I have reference has no proper connection with the Justice Department, that it does not originate in and is not written by any attache of the department, by any employee of the department, it is not printed in the government printing office, it has no place in the machinery of this goverment, in the routine of this government at all, except when it has come in from the outside to the Justice Department with the idea of having the stamp affixed which will enable it to beat its wav-through the Canadian mail. Now, I think it is a particularly aggravated case that a public department such as the Justice Department, which of all others should not lend itself to any infraction of the revenue laws of this country, which should be the most zealous to protect the revenue, should be engaged in a scheme to defraud the revenue. It seems a monstrous thing that this department should lend itself to an object of this kind; and the conviction is forced upon us that it is not an accident that the Justice Department is so used, but that the persons who choose this agency do it because of their belief that they' are better protected from prosecution than they would be if they were dealing by any other department. When this matter was before the House last year what seemed to be a bold challenge was thrown out by the Solicitor General. 'I have done no wrong ' he said; but if I have done wrong, whv does the hon. gentleman not prosecute me5' An easy challenge made with the acclaim of his colleagues in this House that I very well remember.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The challenge was not issued to my colleagues, but to the members who were making the charge on the other side of the House.

Precisely, I think that is what I said. But I am glad that the Solicitor General has repeated now what Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
I think I may desecribe as a raw bluff. The reason I use that term is this, that the Solicitor General is an officer high in the legal service of this country, and he at lea,st is presumed to know the law. The Postal Act prescribes certain procedure in connection with the prosecution of offences under the Act. Section 137 has this provision:
Every pecuniary penalty imposed by this Act, or by any regulation of the Postmaster General made under it, shall be recoverable with costs by the Postmaster General, by civil action in any court of competent jurisdiction, and shall belong to His Majesty for the public uses of Canada, saving always the power of the Governor in Council to allow any part or the whole of such penalty to the officer or person by whose information or intervention the same was recovered.
I have read this Act carefully and I cannot see that any person other than the Postmaster General has any authority to institute _ prosecutions under it. Therefore, I say it is nothing but a raw bluff when the Solicitor General, who must be presumed to know the law, stands up here and distinctly exempts the Postmaster General from the terms of his challenge, when he says, I challenge any person else in this House, except the one authorized to prosecute me, to institute a prosecution. Now it is because the Postmaster General is the one person authorized to act under this section that I propose to call upon him to take such action. I would like, before I offer the resolution so calling upon the Postmaster General, to illumine the House as to the nature of this literature which is being distributed by the Justice Department, to call the attention of the House to one circular sent out which I have here, and which I will offer as a sample of the mendacious character of this literature. To show how resolute is this determination to put a stop to race-track gambling let me read this paragraph:

A question asked by the Department of Justice. I would like to call the attention of the clean-minded non-gambling portion of the community to the contrasting fact that the record of this House will show that the Minister of Justice himself stated from his seat that gambling on race-tracks is not an evil. It seems to me that the advice of the Minister 2474
of Justice was more potent than any other agency in this House in securing the defeat of the Bill which that circular from the Department of Justice represents to the people of Canada as being opposed particularly by the Tory race-track owners, when it was opposed particularly with more authority, with more influence, because of their position in this House by the Minister of Justice, whose department, sends out this mendacious statement, and by his colleague, the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). If the people of Canada understand! that they must wake up to a realization of the fact that the Liberals have lost control of the House of Commons, because if such were tire attitude of the Liberal party it is within our recollection that they very signally failed in carrying it out. The people of Canada will understand that the Liberals are in favour of abolishing ra cotrack gambling and that two leading Conservatives in the House, Messrs. Osier and Barker, both interested in race-tracks, are opposed to the reforms suggested, notwithstanding the attitude of public opinion on the subject.
When I observed that that circular and others like it were being sent out from that department it occurred to me that surely no person in high responsibility there could be cognizant of it. I pictured the righteous indignation of the Minister of Justice when his attention should be called to the subject. I had in my mind the top lofty way in which we would get the reply from him that here was an hon. member of this House tilting perhaps against a messenger or a chief messenger in the department who had affixed this offending stamp. Realizing the way in which the franking privilege was conducted in the department, I took the precaution of putting a question on the order paper to ask what official of the department was responsible for the admin-

istration of the franking privilege, and who is charged with the duty of seeing that no abuse is permitted under it. The answer 1 got precludes the responsibility being shifted by the Minister of Justice upon any messenger or menial of the department. The answer was that the franks of the Justice Department are those of the Minister of Justice, the Solicitor General and the deputy minister, and that the deputy minister is the person responsible for the administration, to see that no abuses take place under it. I have too much Tespect for the Deputy Minister of Justice to entertain the idea for a moment that this thing is done under his responsibility. While the responsibility is technically his, yet in the Department of Justice the Minister and the Solicitor General outrank the deputy minister, and I think the responsibility must be placed higher up. It is not for me to say whether or not it should be placed with the gentleman whose name appears as the frank upon these documents. It is for the Postmaster General, as I take it, upon the information given to him and which has been for long in; his possession; it is for him to find out who it is who illegally puts that stamp on matter purporting to indicate it is entitled to pass free of postage, when it is not so entitled. The questions asked and answered last year show that this practice had been going on from the 20th April, 1907, to the 27th November of the same year, a period of 30 weeks, and from July 21, 1908, to January 19, 1909, a period of 26 weeks, making 56 weeks thus far, and then there has been a recess during which this practice has continued for 24 weeks, making a total of 80 weeks in all. Another answer said that the circulars sent out averaged from 75 to 100 weekly. We must take it that the department put the best face upon it, and we are entitled to assume that 100 per week i- the average number sent out, so that during that period of 80 weeks there have been 8,000 offences committed against the Postal Act by somebody in the Justice Department. I want to call attention to a clause in the Postal Act which shows that the burden of proof in such a case is not unon any private member of the House or upon any citizen of the country to show beyond a shadow of a doubt that some one in the Justice Depai'tment has incurred a very serious penaltv. The burden on the contrary is placed, by section 138 of the Postal Act, upon the person accused :
In any action or proceeding for the recovery of postage or of any penalty under this Act, the burden of proof that the thing alleged to have been done by the defendant was done in conformity to or without violation of this Act, shall lie upon the defendant.
Therefore, under this Act which is made to grind the public, which is made to make Mr. J. D. TAYLOR.
it beyond peradventure that if any citizen of this country is accused of writing a line inside a newspaper and sending that out at newspaper postage and that line is found, he shall be held prima facie guilty of having .written that line and to have committed an offence against the Postal Act. And. under that section of the Act, the citizens of Canada are constantly being haled before Post Office inspectors all over this Dominion and are being fined because there is a prima facie case against them. The department is not bound to establish that they are guilty, but it is up to the accused to establish they are not guilty. Therefore, I say it is up to whoever in the Justice Department affixes this stamp to matter of the nature I have indicated, to prove beyond peradventure that he has the right under the law to do it, or else to be placed in the same position as other private citizens and to suffer the penalty described in this Act. Mr. Speaker, when this matter was before the House last time we permitted it to be disposed of on the promise by the Postmaster General that regulations would be adopted to make it impossible for the offences to be continued. speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to say at the outset that while I have the pleasure of some acquaintance with the piece of political news print which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) has exhibited in the House and has read to the great delight of his friends who sit about him, I have not seen any copies of that news print for a great many months and I have not at any time sent to anybody any such document or any copy of it. I do not know anything about its history, its origin, or the source from which it may have been supplied to the hon. gentleman who has utilized it this morning. But I want in that connection to say further: It seems to please hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House at times when it suits their purpose, to erect the Minister of Justice or the Department of Justice upon some sort of pedestal or throne, setting up that' department as though it were a sort of guardian or

keeper over the consciences of the other departments, and of the other members of this government. I wish to say, so far as I am concerned, that I think there is no warrant whatever for attempting any such position on the part of hon. gentlemen either in this House or out of this House. I think myself it was a misfortune that in the framing of our constitution 40 years ago the good old title ' Attorney General' was dropped and the continental appellation 'Minister of Justice' substituted for it. The Department of Justice, if I understand its end, is simply the legal department of His Majesty's government in Canada. It is literally the department of the Attorney General; the Minister of Justice to my understanding of that term is simply the general attorney of the people of Canada. And so far as the present incumbent of that office is concerned I want to say further, that lie makes no pretense of being put upon any higher plane than his colleagues in this government or his colleagues who are members of this House. For myself,
I think myself a politician. I am not seeking to put myself upon any higher footing; I am a political partisan.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If any gentlemen on the other side of the House wish to call each other by some more high sounding appellation; if they Wish to consider each other statesmen and not politicians they are welcome to do so. I. have to say that so far as I am concerned I think it no discredit to be called a politician, to be called a political partisan, and to be prepared to take any share I am able to take in the political warfare of my colleagues and of my party.
Now, with regard to the subject which the hon. gentleman has brought to the attention of the House, so far as I am personally concerned I should be very glad to see the franking privilege in this country abolished. I do not know what merit there is in it. I think it is a system which has been in the past abused, and which it would be better in the public interest should be abolished. But, I found it in force when I took charge of the Post Office Department five years ago. I did not remain in charge of that department long enough to work any startling revolutions in its administration, and I do not know if I had proposed that the franking privilege should be abolished that I would have received much support from any hon. gentleman in this House. But taking the provisions of the law on the subject as they stand, I want to point out what I understand them to be, and to ask each member of the House who is accustomed to exercise his privileges in that respect, conscientiously to inquire of himself whether or not he is in a position to throw any stones in this matter. ^ I had not been long in this House or in the position of Postmaster General of Canada when a member of this House came ^to me one day-a member whom I had 'never seen before and who is not a political friend-and asked me to give him my frank as Postmaster General. I told him I had not any except my hand-writing. He answered that would do, and he asked me to come with him to the parliamentary post office and put my initials as Postmaster General on some mailable matter that the post office authorities would not carry for him upon his own initials. I went with him, hardly understanding what the difficulty could be, but I understood when I found what I was wanted to do. I was wanted to frank through His Majesty mails a bag full of grain.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I did it, and I suppose the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Taylor) would like to have me and his friends who sit in this House on the same side of it as himself, prosecuted as criminals for that act.

Mr. Speaker, if I may presume to instruct the Minister of Justice on the larv, I would say to him that there is no limitation on the right of a member of parliament to frank any matter that is at all mailable; he is different from an employee or an official of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. gentleman's idea would not avail if he went into a court prosecuting in the case I have described. If the hon. gentleman thinks that the law is such that any member of the House is entitled to frank through the mails of this country, free of charge, bags of grain, or his wardrobe, I think he will find himself mistaken.
Mr. Speaker
Order; sit down.

If gentlemen opposite will keep order; I rise, as I have the privilege to rise, and say that the hon. gentleman who has the floor is misstating, perhaps not intentionally, what I have said. I did not say anything of the kind which he attributes to me. I said that any member of this House has the right to frank any matter which is mailable.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I purpose, Mr. Speaker, calling attention to the provisions of the law on the subject in a minute or two, but in reference to the incident to which I have been adverting, I want simply to remind the hon. gentleman who has been interrupting me, that if there

liad been no infraction of the law in what I was being asked as Postmaster General to do, there was no occasion to come to me in the matter, because the hon. gentleman who wanted to nse the mails for the carriage of his bag of grain could have franked it himself. And it was simply because he was transgressing the regulations, and knew he was transgressing the regulations, that he came to me, asking me as Postmaster General to direct my officials to do for me that which they would not do for him. Now, one hears a good deal in the way of rumour around the hafls and the lobbies as to what is going on from day to day during the session on the part of hon. members of this House in the way of sending things through the mails. I do not intend to talk about that; I think in these matters there is not very much involved, and it is just as well that there should be some idea on both sides of the House of applying the ancient principle of noblesse oblige. And there are things in regard to which if there be transgressions of the strict letter of the law, it is very doubtful if it is in the public interest that there should be attention called to them and discussion had of them. I do not understand that the franking privilege of a member of this House during the session is any wider or any different from the like privileges to the departments of the government during the recess. The statute is that which governs. I am not particularly concerned with the Post Office regulations. So far as they are based upon the statute, so far as they are not contradictory to the statute, so far as they are authorized by the statute they are of course the rules upon which the Post Office Department, and the officials of that department, must carry on their business. But, no department of this government, b,y any regulations it may promulgate, not the whole government or His Excellency in Council, have any right to take from a member of this House that which is given him by the statute which preserves the right of a member and the right of a minister in the matter of exercising the franking privilege.
Section 75 of the Post Office Act, limiting it to this particular matter, directs that all mailable matter sent by any department of the government, at the seat of government, shall be free of postage. The corresponding section with regard to members limits their franking privilege to the duration of the session, otherwise it is practically in the same -words. As to members, 'all mailable matter addressed by,' is the expression, 'addressed by any member of either House at the seat of government during the session of parliament is entitled to be carried free.' I think there is a good deal of misconception on this subject. I have heard or seen that hon.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
members have spoken with the idea that ten days after or before the session they are in the same position as during the session. I see no warrant for that idea whatever. Mailable matter may be sent to any member free of charge during ten days before a session, but so far as anything sent out by a member is concerned, his right of franking is limited to the duration of the session and his right of franking is conferred by the law, in almost identical words with the departmental rights of franking mentioned in the other section. It is all mailable matter, in one case sent by any department, in the other, addressed by any member. And you have simply the situation that whatever a member during a session may address, a department at all time of the year may send. Now, with regard to the Department of Justice and its administration, I am, by law, made the official who presides over that department. The Solicitor General is by statute assigned the duty of assisting in the litigation of that department. He is my colleague. I do not consider that he is my subordinate. I certainly would think I was guilty of a piece of impudence if I asked him to submit to me his correspondence or undertook to revise his use of his frank. I have no more right to do it in his case than in the case of any other one of my colleagues, and no more right to do it in the case of the Solicitor General, than he has to do it with regard to my correspond-ehce. So far as the department is concerned, using that word as distinguished from the minister and the Solicitor General at the head of the department, so far as clerks in the department are concerned, and the ordinary departmental work, the frank which is used and used so far as I am aware exclusively, is that of the deputy minister. I think he has a stamp. I have never seen it, but I have no doubt he has; I have seen impressions of one, and I understand that the clerks of the department or the messengers of the department in taking to the post office the mailable matter of the day, affix the stamp of the deputy minister. So far as I am concerned, I have no stamp. I frank by writing with my pen, or my secretary writes with his pen my initials in the corner of the envelope. That system is pursued in regard, to whatever letters I dictate during the day, whether it is session or not session. Some of these letters, I am afraid, are upon political subjects. Some of these letters, it may be, do not concern the business of the Department of Justice. Once in a while I write a letter to my son; possibly I may write to my good old father. It is not upon departmental business, and I do not put postage stamps on such letters. If I am wrong, I am in the judgment of this House, and I hope my friend to whom 1

sent a bagful of oats a few years ago won't be the first man to condemn me.
Mr. Speaker
Order.
I think from the pointed manner in which the hon. gentleman threw that bagful of oats I should state that I did not ask him to frank them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am sorry the hon. gentleman thought it necessary to make that observation. I took good care to tell the House that it was during the few months I was Postmaster General that it occurred, and unless my recollection is very erroneous my hon. friend did not represent New Westminster at that time. It was not the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Taylor). Now, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the political literature that has been discussed here, I do not suppose it goes out under my initials. It certainly does not go out under my initials to nay knowledge. If my secretary, or his assistant has any part in mailing the kind of document that has been referred to I do not know anything about it. I do not think that is the fact, nor do I think that it is the fact that any official of the department using the departmental stamp of the deputy minister is engaged in sending out literature of the character described, or anything of a political nature. As to what the Solicitor General may do under his own signature, or under his own frank, I do not conceive that I am entitled to inquire, any more than I am entitled to inquire into the mailable correspondence of any member of this House during the session. On the principle on which it is argued that the correspondence of the Solicitor General, or of the Minister of Justice ought to be inspected, it is, I suppose, contended that envelopes are to be opened, and that one ought to see whether or not in the envelope which is sealed up, and is franked with the minister's name, or the name of the Solicitor General, there is something contraband. If that is the principle the hon. gentleman is contending for, if that is what he wants the House to accept by the motion he has made, I hope he will have the frankness to let us know, so that we will not be asked to express ourselves upon this question without understanding whether or not every member of this House is to submit his personal correspondence to some official, or to some minister, or to some authority to see whether or not it contains something which he ought not to send out. Well, Sir, in regard to this whole matter I do not ' care to express any opinion as to the magnitude which it may assume in the minds of hon. gentlemen. Each member of the House will form his own opinion about that. I simply want to put it as I have
tried to do upon tin language ot the law. My position is }hat during the recess every minister in connection with his department, every department, has identically the same franking right that every member has during the session. There is nothing in the statute about departmental business. It is mailable matter, and any mailable matter any minister has the right under the law to frank on any day of the year. Change the law as soon as you please. I am perfectly prepared to support any proposal to strike out every one of those clauses from the statute. They do not have the franking privilege in England. Members of parliament there pay their own postage, and I think members here could do it also. But, as long as the law remains as it is, and as long as members of this House are entitled to put their frank during the session upon any letter they like, whether it concerns private, political, or other business-whether it is their letter, or the letter of some member of their family; whether it is the letter of their own family, or the letter of some friend; whether it is even the member's initials upon the corner of an envelope in blank and handed to a man who asks for it of him on the street exactly as he would ask for a postage stamp-*as long as the law remains in that position it is not-I had almost said not consistent with the dignity of this House-to occupy hours of the time of the House in discussing such a matter as this.

I think that the Minister of Justice should be the guardian of the dignity of this House. He is the minister to whom we have a right to look for the embodiment of the highest moral tone in our public life. But when a man in such a position will rise in his place in this House and acknowledge himself - to be a political partisan, as he has just done, the dignity of the House needs some other protection. I can only say that we on this side of the House have for many years been of exactly the opinion now expressed by the Minister of Justice. But though we have always regarded that hon. gentleman as a political partisan, 1 never thought that the time would come when one occupying that position would openly acknowledge in his place in this House that this was his character. But the indictment presented by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) was so strong, so conclusive, that there was absolutely no use in longer attempting concealment of the fact that the present Minister of Justice is a political partisan.
Now, it seems to me that the question before the House is a very important matter. It came up in the House last session,

and I took some small part in the discussion. The Postmaster General (Mr. Le-mieux) at that time gave us a very lair promise-and I was delighted on that occasion with the speech he made. For, had he carried out the promises he gave, we should find him to-day voting for the resolution presented by my hon. friend from New Westminster. Let me read briefly from the debate on that occasion. In the course of my address I used these words:
If the Post Office Act does not provide some penalty for a man who unjustly uses the franking privilege, it is high time that an amendment was brought in to make it a criminal offence for any person to use the franking privilege who has not authority to do so.
The Postmaster General said:
I may say at once that the supposed franks which have been exhibited this afternoon reveal a state of things which I will not tolerate.
And he went on:
At all events I say that this state of things cannot be tolerated because the Post Office Department must have the respect of all parties in this country, and I intend for the future to see that the spirit and the letter of the law shall be carried o^t. . . . We will frame such regulations as in the future only purely official business bearing the frank of ministers and members of parliament will go through the mails. I may say. that since the beginning of the session I have received complaints from certain firms in reference to the abuse of the franking privilege. I attribute the reason for these complaints to the fact that it was done by new members of the House.
Now, I hold in my hand an envelope addressed to the ' Advocate,' a paper published at Balgonie, Sask., in which was contained a copy of the literature part of which was read by my hon. friend from New Westminster. This bears the postmark of Ottawa and upon the envelope the signature ' Jacques Bureau.' It is postmarked March 14, 1910. So when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) contends that he does not know that this is done by any official of his department, we must assume that that is true; but now that we have brought the matter to his attention his plea of ignorance cannot hold. It is shown that this kind of literature-I cannot call it anything but Ananias literature-is being circulated at the public expense. I say that it is a disgrace to this country, and it is a disgrace to the Department of Justice to play the part of a political partisan in sending this literature throughout the country. The statements contained in that literature are so contrary to the facts that I cannot characterize it in words strong enough. We all know that the speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) was the very Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
cause of the defeat of the Anti-Race Track Gambling Bill. The idea that notwithstanding this fact, which is known to us all, this literature should contain statements that the government were doing their best to pass the Bill and to further the measures against race-track gambling. Why, before such literature the reputation of Ananias melts like snow before the spring-tide sun. I ask the Postmaster General to tell us whether he has taken any steps to implement the promise he made a year ago to the members of this House upon the faith of which the discussion was ended. We took the hon. gentleman at his word; we supposed that he would make regulations which would prevent-even if the present regulations cannot prevent, which we say they can-the continuation of this abuse. Has he taken steps to prevent a repetition of that which was shown to exist last year, and will he take steps to prevent what has been shown to exist here to-day?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Last year, when this question was brought up, I made the remark that was quoted by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro). He will remember that I was shown some letters which were supposed to have been franked by some members of the government. Experts on both sides of the House looked at the initials, and not one could say whose initials they were. I then stated that this was certainly an abuse-that, evidently, some signatures had been used illegally, forged in effect, and that I would see to it that such a thing could not occur again. My hon. friend will remember that I handed to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) an envelope which was supposed to contain a political pamphlet distributed during the period of the general election in one of the constituencies-Dufferin, I think-and the minister (Mr. Fisher) peremptorily observed that the signature was not his. It was upon that occasion that I declared that if such a thing occurred again I would take prompt measures to stop it. Now, let us be frank.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, and let us not frank as some hon. members on the other side frank at the general election. Now, will it be seriously contended for one moment that a member of this House has not the right, during the session of parliament, to send letters to his constituents and others, using for that purpose the franking privilege which he gets under the law-for, under the statute all mailable matter can be franked during the session by a member of the House.
That would include a bag of oats?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. gentleman understands the definition of ' mailable matter.' If an hon. gentleman gave his frank on that occasion, I suppose he thought that the bag of oats could pass in His Majesty's mails. Can it be contended for a moment that whilst the members of the House during session are given by law the privilege of sending abroad tons of literature, a member of the government shall not have the privilege of sending letters under his own frank during recess? Now, as was well said by the Minister of Justice, and as every lawyer knows, no regulation can destroy'the effect of a statute passed by this House. Section 75 enacts that:
All letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Governor General, or sent to or by any department of the government at the seat of government, shall be free of Canadian postage under such regulations as are from time to time made in "that respect by the Governor in Council.
I am prompted by my hon. friend from New Westminster to quote again section 114 of the regulations, which reads as follows :
All letters and other mailable matter sent by the public departments at Ottawa and franked as being of a departmental character, all , correspondence addressed to the ministers in charge of the said departments or to their private secretaries, or to the deputy heads or secretaries of the same, or to any recognized branch or division of a department.	[DOT]
All these enjoy the franking privilege. Now, I will ask, is there a distinction between letters sent personally by a minister and a letter of a departmental character? Before I do it., I must explain the raison d'etre of these regulations, and I believe every business man in the House will understand it. In order to prevent civil servants from abusing the franking privilege given by law to the departments, we had to frame a regulation that the letters sent from those departments through the mail must be of a departmental character. But as the Minister of Justice well says, we cannot, in the Post Office Department, set aside what has been enacted by this parliament in the Revised Statutes, section 75, which I have read.
Shall be free under the regulations.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, under the regulations. Will my hon. friend, who I know is a lawyer of distinction in his province, contend that under the statute and the regulations I have read, a minister of the Crown is debarred from the privilege of franking his letters during recess? Why,
my hon. friend could not plead such a contention in any court of the land. My hon. friend thinks perhaps that the Solicitor General does not enjoy the franking privilege. Now, although his name is not mentioned in the statute, he is however, as the Minister of Justice stated, considered a member of the government, although he is not a member of the cabinet. But let me tell my hon. friend this, that three years ago, by an order in council passed by this government, the Solicitor General was given the franking privilege. Now, I appeal to my hon. friend, the leader of the opposition, I appeal to his sense of justice and to his sense of fair play: will he tell me-I have just seen the envelope which was handed to me by my hon. friend the member for Frontenac, bearing the signature. of the Solicitor General-will the leader of the opposition, who is a lawyer of great distinction, and for whom I have the greatest respect, tell me, as -was said a moment ago by the member for New Westminster, that the Solicitor General has been violating the law in the spirit and in the letter, and that he is amenable to the courts under section 119 of the Post Office Act? Can it be for a moment contended that he has, in the words of that section:
Forged, counterfeited, or unlawfully imitated, used or affixed, to or upon any letter or packet, any stamp, signature, initials, or other mark or sign purporting that such letter or package ought to pass free of postage, or at a lower rate of postage, or that the postage thereon or any part thereof has been prepaid or ought to be paid by or charged to any person or department.
It seems to me it is not even necessary to discuss that question. The statute is very clear. During the session of parliament, every member is given by law the franking privilege, he can send letters and parcels of the prescribed size mentioned in the regulations, he can send all mailable matter. Now, during recess, during tire whole year round, the members of the government are given the same privilege.
No. Will the Postmaster General quote the section of the Act giving that privilege?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
It is given in section 75:
All letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Governor General, or sent to or by any department of the government at the seat of government, shall be free of Canadian postage.
Is not the minister the head of the department, are not his letters letters of the department?
Will the minister read the remainder of the section?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
-shall be free of Canadian postage under such regulations as are from time to time made in that respect by the Governor in Council.
Regulations made in order to stop any abuse which might be committed in the size of the mailable matter, or sending such articles as a bag of oats, for instance, or a wardrobe, and many other things that civil servants had been sending for years, in abuse of their privilege, perverting the sense of the Act, and we had to put a stop to it. Now, nobody will contend that any bar has been put to the free exercise of that privilege by members of the House. I remember that, during the session preceding the last general election and during every session preceding a general election since I have had a seat in this House, my hon. friend the member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), who had charge of the literature of his political party, jammed for weeks and months, the corridors and lobbies of this House with literature destined to be sent to the independent electors of this country. We did not object and we do not object to-dayi 'We are given the same privilege on this side of the House. Will any one say, with the law as it stands, with the regulations as they exist, the object of which I gave a moment ago, because the Solicitor General sends, under his _ franking privilege at certain intervals during the year and during the recess, the envelopes which weTe shown a moment ago, the Postmaster General should interpose and order those letters to be opened?
Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That I should do that.
Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I would not stay in the government ten minutes if I were to do that.
The hon. member would stay in any other government if he did that.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: There is no chance of my hon. friend ever coming at the head of any government with the ideas that he has propounded to-day.

I would like to asis the Postmaster General, if, in view of the law and knowing that literature of the character which has been referred to in this House has been franked with the frank of the Solicitor General, he approves of the transaction?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Mv hon. friend has put a question to me. I am not here to speak for the Solicitor General. He is here and I suppose he will be heard from during this debate.
Will the minister take any steps to prevent that?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I certainly say that to my mind there has been no trespass of the law under the circumstances.
May I ask the Postmaster General if, having heard the literature read, he thinks it is proper literature to send out?
Oh, oh.

I do not rise to make any argument upon this resolution; I simply rise to make an explanation. I do not wish to have it generally understood that all members of this House are guilty of sending a bag of oats to their constituents, but I simply want to explain the whole circumstances and I will leave to the judgment of the House whether or not I transgressed the law. The Minister of Justice and the Postmaster General can verify the facts which I anj about to state if they wish to go to the trouble. A good Liberal in my constituency, by the name of John Perry, and residing at Treherne, wrote to me and asked if I thought it would be possible to get a couple of bushels of oats in order that he might sow a plot of land and thereby be of some benefit to his fellow farmers by distributing the seed. I took his letter, read it over the 'phone to Dr. Saunders of the Experimental Farm and asked him if he would supply that quantity of oats. He replied that he would be pleased to comply with the request as contained in the letter. I heard nothing more of it until I came up to the building one morning and found a bag of oats in room 6. The other members began laughing, and I said: What shall I do with it? They did not know. I went to the postmaster, Mr. Mills, and I told him that I had this bag of oats. I said that I could comply with the law by breaking it up into small parcels and sending them out, as the Experimental Farm sends out small samples of grain of a certain weight. He said there was another way in which 1 might succeed in getting it through, that if I got the Postmaster General's frank it would go. I met the Postmaster General in the lobby and lie was kind enough, in the interest of agriculture in this country, to walk into the post office with me and attach his frank to the bag, and that is the last I heard of it until it landed in Treherne. I would just like to say that that innocent bag of oats sent out to produce good innocent material for this country is quite different from the letters which have, been read. I have no doubt the government expect these letters that they sent, out to bear fruit, as I expected this bag of oats that I sent out to bear fruit, but I do not believe that all the hon. members

of both sides of this House desire to obtain votes with any such literature as that which has been read here this morning. Misrepresentation of facts, fabrication- nothing could be further from the facts as regards the Gambling Bill than the statements contained in that circular. The Minister of Justice and every other member of this House knows the way that Bill was dealt with. The Minister of Justice and the right hon. First Minister know how that Bill was killed, and they know it was killed by the Minister of Justice, who has been so driven for an argument to defend that literature as to refer to this bag of oats that went through the mails. If he can find any justification for the sending out of that literature under the frank of his department by referring to this b.ag of oats then I hope he will enjoy whatever advantage he may get out of it.

We have had rather a good natured discussion. Some men appear to have felt their oats, some have made wry faces, others have talked about small potatoes and others have been accused of being dead beats.
Good, good.

Very good. A particular letter has been referred to and the statements contained in it, it has been said, would have done credit to Annanias. I suppose that that could have been said of a great- deal of the literature sent out by our^ friends on the other side of the House dui'ing the last campaign. I remember some of that literature. I did not intend to commit it to memory, but I remember that it bore a very good picture of the very good looking leader of the opposition and one statement contained in it was that the Conservatives had endeavoured to abolish or reduce to 10 per cent the duty on agricultural implements, but that they had been prevented by members sitting on the Liberal side of the House from doing so. If anything more Ananias-like than that has ever been sent out by any party in the Dominion of Canada within the last century I would like to know about it.
Was there not a vote on the motion to reduce the duty on agricultural implements?

Yes, I refhember the vote very well. I remember that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) his then first lieutenant, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and a number of other leading Conservatives voting against him, and I remember that my hon. friend who has just sat down and a few others, representing rural constituencies on the other side of the House, voted for it.
How did you vote?
I voted against it because I thought it was a hypocritical resolution
Order, order.
-that would not do any credit to any man or to any party, and it did less credit to the party who used it in their campaign literature.

I
have in my possession one of these effusions sent out as Liberal campaign literature, and among other things there is a reference in it to myself. It says that the member for Frontenac stated that the French Canadians were disloyal, and I want to say that- to attribute to me such a statement is an absolute falsehood. It ill becomes the position held by the Solicitor General to allow his frank to be used in sending throughout the country an absolute lie such as that is. We have been treated to some surprises this morning, but before referring to them, allow me to *make a brief reference to this lying statement in that pamphlet. I can only conceive two reasons why a statement like that should be sent broadcast through the country. One of these reasons is that it is easier for the Liberal party or those who got up the pamphlet-I am not now accusing the Solicitor General of having prepared it-but it was easier for the Liberal party to attempt to draw a herring across the scent and try to make the people of Quebec believe that I was attacking the masses of the people of that province than it was to defend the Prime Minister and the leaders of the party whom I indicted. Another Teason which occurs to me is that possibly by the circulation of such lies as this they think to provoke me into saying something against the people of the province of Quebec, but in that attempt they wall be just as unsuccessful as in their other attempt.
You have said enough already.

Not the least surprise we have had this morning was that afforded by the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller). I would expect if there was one member on the other -side who would have kept his silence on this question it would have been the hon. gentleman. I would like to ask him, he who talks about hypocrisy and hypocritical literature, what trait of his character he is exhibiting in regard to the attitude of the Minister of Justice on his anti-gambling Bill. I would like to ask him if he approves of that statement in that pamphlet in reference to the gambling Bill? Did be prepare these statements himself and send them out? The fact is that it is very apparent to every member of this House that the Minister of Justice

780S
got up in his place and was the means of defeating the Miller anti-gambling Bill, and, notwithstanding that, the member for Grey rises now to add his little quotation in the way of excuse for the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Justice waxed highly indignant at the very thought that his department should be regarded for one moment as the guardian of the other departments of the government. Well, Sir, we who have had the privilege of one or two short sessions in this House, and have had an opportunity of looking into the doings of this government, would sympathize with the Minister of Justice if such a burden were cast upon him, but I venture to think that after the display of the Minister of Justice this morning there are yet some departments of this government which would pray to be relieved of his guardianship. We have had ample evidence of the partisan disposition of the Minister of Justice, but it remained for himself to rise in his place in the House and to tell us that he, the head of that department which is supposed to be as far removed from political bias as it is possible to get a department, that he is a political partisan, and that he glories in the fact. The Minister of Justice made considerable out of the statement that one of the members of this House asked him to frank a bag of oats through the mail. I would have supposed that the Minister of Justice had refused to break the regulations and the law, but he went on to tell us that he did break the regulations and that he did the very thing, which as head of the Department of Justice, he should not have done. Imagine the head of the Department of Justice taking pride in the fact that he himself broke the law. What a nice Minister of Justice. Now, Sir, it is true, as the Postmaster General has said, that members of parliament and members of the government have the right to use the franking privilege, but the Postmaster General has not dealt fairly with the . question, because after saying that members of the government send their mail matter out under regulations, he did not tell us that the regulations say:	'and
frank as being of an official character.' The Postmaster General slid over that point. What the regulations do say is that this mail matter must be of an official character, and if it is not of an official character and the members of the government send it out under a frank then they stand convicted of violation of the laws they are supposed to maintain.

I do not rise to complain of the statement of the Minister of Justice that the Department of Justice of this country at the present time is on no higher plane than any department of the government, Mr. EDWARDS.
nor do I complain of the accuracy of his statement that it is administered under its present head by as violent a political partisan as there is in the government. But, Sir, I had understood until now that one of the functions of the Justice Department was to make clear to this House the real meaning of the law. To-day it has discharged that function by obscuring where-ever it could the plainest possible law, and with the assistance of the Postmaster General endeavouring to befuddle the members of this House as to what the departmental regulations mean. Nothing could be clearer than what the law means; it does not need a lawyer to interpret it. Section 75 says that mail matter of any kind may be sent to or from members of parliament at any time during the session, and it does not matter what that mail matter is. The Minister of Justice tried to obscure the issue by implying that it was a violation of the law for a member of the House to frank a letter to one's father, but, of course, that is not so. There is no violation either of the spirit or the letter of the law in franking such a -letter as that. It is also contained in section 75 that during recess matter may be sent at any time to or from departments of this government under such regulations as the Postmaster General provides. These words mean something or they mean nothing. They are a notification that the Post Office Department has authortiy to make regulations covering the sending of literature to and from the departments of this government, and the Post Office Department has made such regulations. Those regulations either mean something or they mean nothing. The Postmaster General, who I regret to say, departed from his usual custom and did not have the courage in this House to express his own convictions; the Postmaster General endeavoured meekly to reconcile himself with the attitude of the Minister of Justice in arguing that this regulation wras beyond the power of the department. What a position for the Post- , master General to take.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I did not say it was beyond the power of the Post Office Department to enact regulations. I read the regulation, and I said there was no contradiction between the regulations and the statute. I might explain that the employees are warned not to mix their personal letters with departmental letters. I may add that in every department the letters are collected every afternoon and they are deposited in the ante-room of the deputy minister and only the frank of the deputy minister and the frank of the minister are used on the letters. No other franks are used in the department.

I perhaps did the Postmaster General too much justice in stating
7S09

that he argued practically that this regulation was beyond the powers of his department to enact. But he did not conflict with the statement of the Minister of Justice that no regulation could obviate or get around the provisions of an Act of parliament, and he, therefore, conveyed the impression to this House that in his mind this regulation was ultra vires of his department. I say that the regulation is not ultra vires of his department, and that it is absolutely within the power of his department to make. The regulation says that during recess., mail matter may be sent out by the department if it is of an official character. Now, then, does it make or does it not make it clear that the matter sent out must be of an official character? If it does not mean that the matter sent out must be of an official character, the regulation means nothing whatever, and the Postmaster General knows it. If anything at all can be sent out hv that department and franked by the department as ' official,' then the regulation might be just as well omitted altogether.
At one o'clock, House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, by reading section 1X4 of the regulations in conjunction with clause 75 of the Act, it is made abundantly clear to every one, the regulation being within the power of the department, that to frank mail matter that is not departmental from the department at any time, whether _ during the recess, or during the session, is a violation of the law. It is abundantly clear, - also, that to frank mail matter of any kind, departmental or otherwise, to a member during the session is not a violation of the law. That is just the difference. Now it is either right or it is wrong to send the literature quoted in this House as official matter. If it is departmental matter, it has a right to be franked as such, and it is not a violation of the law. If it is not departmental matter, it is a violation of the law to frank it as such, and send it out. Now from that position the Postmaster General cannot dissent, nor can any other person dissent. It is as clear as any section of law ever written that to frank out matter of that sort as departmental matter either during the session, or during the recess by a department is a violation of the law. IJ can he franked out during the session by a member of parliament, but it cannot be franked out even during a session by a department without violating the law, and it is violating the law with double clearness when it is so franked out during recess at which time it cannot be legally franked either by a member of parliament, or by a department. Consequently the Postmaster General is face to face with this position', that
not a private man, not a mere private citizen, but the Liberal party of this House, and of this country is openly, under his eyes, violating the section that he is sworn to enforce. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is the position the Postmaster General is in. But the situation is worse. What is the class of literature that is being so franked, and from whom does it emanate? In the first place the literature sent out in that way is an official leaflet of the Liberal party of Canada. It is the official organ of the Liberal members of parliament of this House. It is literature of which the government itself takes advantage, and seeks to take advantage. It is literature which it is hoped will help to re-elect hon. members opposite at the next election. That is its purpose; it has no other. Now, Mr. Speaker, to call that literature lies, is to award it undue euphony. The Minister of Justice is in his seat. The Postmaster General is in his seat. There are scores of Liberal members of this House in their seats, and there is not one of them who will stand in his place now and say that the references in that leaflet are not lies, deliberate lies. It is not only a lie, but a pernicious despicable lie of the worst character. It is not only deceit, Mr. Speaker, but cowardly deceit, and still the Minister of Justice rises in his place in the House, he knows it has been sent out, and sent out illegally, he knows he is as much the author of it as any other member of the Liberal party in this House, and still in the face of that- he declines to repudiate it or to say one word against it in his speech on this matter. Now, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice, I stated in the first place, endeavoured only to befuddle the House as to the law. The law could not be clearer. What did he say in endeavouring to obscure it? He said it was only a lax enforcement of the law that enabled him to write to his father, or to his son. The minister franking a letter to his father or to his son knows he is acting as much within the law as if he franked out an official letter from his department. The Minister of Justice knows it, and yet he added to the demerits of his defence by calling on the member from Macdonald (Mr. Staples) to explain the franking out of some oats some years ago. I can only gather two facts from that incident. The first one is that the hon. member for Macdonald not being a lawyer committed an illegal Act, and did not know he was doing it.
Oh, oh.

And the second is that the Minister of Justice committed the same illegal act, and knew it was not only wrong, but* illegal.
Arf hon. MEMBER. Hear, hear.

I have it on the information of that hon. member himself (Mr. Staples) that before that bag was so franked, he told the hon. Minister of Justice that he did not want him to frank it if it was in violation of the regulations, and that he did not know until to-day that the franking of that bag of oats was a violation of the regulations. Now, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be truly said that the government of this country are changing their methods in any way. Like others whose principles are against society instead of with society, like the pirate and buccaneer who after long practice of their arts with impunity become reckless in the intoxication of their own success, this government is becoming bolder every hour. Only a short time ago we had the hon. Minister of Finance telling the House that the practice of the patronage system which has done more than anything else to demoralize the political life of this country, was one of the closest things to his own heart, and that the exercise of it was a lasting maxim of his political faith; and to-day when the Minister of Justice is brought face to face with a violation of the law, when he is face to face with a charge that in his own department, under his very eyes, and with his sanction, the law he is sworn to enforce is being violated, when he is further faced with the fact that his department is being prostituted for the basest of party ends, what is the answer he gives to the House? He tells us: I want you to understand that I am at the head of the Justice Department, and I am no statesman, I am a political partisan. Mr. Speaker, if there is one hon. member of this House whose position is less enviable in this matter than any other, it is the hon. member from Grey (Mr. Miller) who introduced the anti-gambling Bill. I supported the anti-gambling Bill. I believed at that time in the hon. gentleman's sincerity. His Bill received, I think, a majority of support from hon. members on this side of the House. The hon. member for Grey knows and has stated that his Bill was defeated by the speech of the hon. Minister of Justice, and yet that hon. member sits here and listens to a lying pamphlet, of which he is as much the author as any other member of this House, and which is intended for his advantage, and he declines to repudiate that pamphlet. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but he actually stands in his place in the House and notwithstanding the fact that the majority on this side of the House supported him he condemns them for their attitude in respect of this pamphlet. Mr. Speaker, allow me to state at the outset that all reproaches or accusations made against the Postmaster General or the Minister of Justice are in my mind not well founded. This letter has been franked, as has been stated, with the frank ' Jacques Bureau.' I have never submitted my correspondence to the Minister of Justice any more than I have submitted it to the Postmaster General. I, and I alone, am responsible for this franking, and, in. justice to both these hon. gentlemen, I assume the responsibility of the whole thing. Now, the charge is that a certain letter written to the newspapers has been franked from the Department of Justice. This letter has been franked, if I am to believe the envelope that stands as convicting evidence against me and which was produced by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) and read as evidence by the hon. memher for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), with the name 'Jacques Bureau' in the lower left hand corner. The hon. member for North Grey says that this letter bears the pestmark Ottawa, 10th March, 1910. I think that on that date, Jacques Bureau, as a member of this House, had as much right to frank a letter as his Conservative friends have to frank the weekly letter that they send out. The letter inclosed in the envelope-I did not have time to Tead it carefully-appears to answer some charges made by the ' Mail and Empire.' This letter wTas mailed December 1, 1909, and on December 1, 1909, this House was in session, and I believe that, as a member of this House, I have as much right to frank the letter-as I have already said-as my hon. friends opposite have to frank their political letters.
Now, I admit that I did use my frank outside of the session. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. J. D. Taylor) may call it a ' raw' bluff ' or whatever he pleases. I used my frank outside the session, and, I claim, used it legally. Hon. members are trying to draw some very fine distinctions about the interpretation of section 75 of the Post Office Act. Now', this section is very plain. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) who is a lawyer, will admit that parliament is supreme and that no Postmaster General can curtail by order in council, any privileges that parliament has given. Now', under what statute do they complain? Under section 75 of the Post Office Act. This is a very old section. Turning to the origin of it, I find that, in 1867, at the time of Confederation, the Post Office Act covered a section having exactly this language the same language as section 75 of the present Act. In 1875, there w'as a consolidation of the Post Office Act. The same language is again used as is used to-day

in tlie consolidated statutes. But, in 1875, the franking privilege of members was enlarged. Up to that time, books sent from the library to members of parliament during the recess, and by members back to the library, had to pay postage, but, in 1875, it was enacted that books transmitted under these conditions should be exempt from postage. I take it that this privilege has been granted to members of parliament because their position necessarily takes them from home and imposes upon them a multiplicity of duties which would not arise in their ordinary calling, thus creating a great deal of correspondence, and, as it is in the interests of the country that this correspondence should be carried on, it was thought wise to exempt members of parliament from the duty of paying postage. I take it also that if a minister of the Crown continues to use his privilege as a member of parliament during the recess under the same conditions as those during session, he ought not to be debarred from that privilege. It has been argued by my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) that the regulations restrict the franking power of members of the departments. I say that, as I read the statute-I may be mistaken; it is a question of interpretation of law, and as I have said, I am not here to advise the House of Commons as to the meaning of the words of the statutes; I may have my own ideas about it, but there are only the courts to decide the case, and no man is bound to agree with me in my opinion; it would be useless to argue a question of law before a tribunal that could not decide upon it-I say that the words granting the privileges to the departments are the same as in the case of members of this House, except that in the latter case it is ' addressed to or by' and, in the former ' sent to or by.' Surely, hon. members opposite will not argue that the effect of the statute is to declare that the words mean that a member may send a thousand or a million letters free if he addresses them during the session or parliament with his own hand. The words must be interpreted fairly. And I claim that the Postmaster General, 'by regulation, cannot curtail any of those powers that are given by the statute, and he cannot curtail them any more in the case of members than he can in the case of the department.
Now, let me read the section again, that I may deal with one or two words in it specially.
All letters and other mailable matter addressed to or sent by the Governor General, or sent to or by any department of the government at the seat of government, shall be free of Canadian postage under such regulations as are from time to time made in that respect by the Governor in Council.
Now, we may have to come down, and discuss here what constitutes a department. As the Minister of Justice has said, in my position as Solicitor General, I do not consider that I am a deputy minister or a civil servant. I consiuer myself, as I might say, the joint head of the Department of Justice, so far as counsel work is concerned, with the Minister of Justice. It is frankly a partnership in which I join in the counsel work with the attorney general who has more extensive powers granted him by the statute. The Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) says that I have certain specified franking privileges by the order in council. Sir, I do not attach so much importance to that after all. I claim that I have the right to frank my letters, and that the order in council is only notice to the postmaster at Ottawa that he is to accept that frank. Would any hon. member on the other side say that he must have in his possession and ready to show to the conductor of a train the certificate of the clerk of the House of Commons in order that he may exercise his right to travel free on a railway train in Canada?
No.
