The statute provides simply two things, one that the matter to be franked must De departmental matter, and in the next place it must be sent out by the department. It is impossible to gainsay that position. There are the clear words of the statute and of the regulation for the consideration of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. Is this departmental matter? The Postmaster General, the Minister of Justice, and the Solicitor General have declared upon their responsibility as ministers of the Crown that the department has absolutely nothing to do with this letter, that they do not know what it is, that they have no conception of its contents. They desire to disassociate themselves from it absolutely, and I congratulate them upon their good taste. They say this has nothing to do with the department. I would like to ask the Postmaster General this. Suppose the Solicitor General or any other official connected with the department sent out a pill advertisement, a patent medicine advertisement, by hundreds of thousands under the frank of the Solicitor General or the Postmaster General, does he say that they would be justified under the terms of this statute and regulation?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: No.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He would not. I would like to know on what higher plane he would put this political letter.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: My hon. friend can surely draw a distinction between political matter and pill advertisements.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Will my hon. friend the Postmaster General point out to me the words of the statute which distinguish between a party political letter and a patent medicine advertisement? I would like to see the language of the statute which makes any such distinction.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will allow me, I stated this morning, and I call to my assistance, if I need any in the present debate, the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. J. Haggart). I stated this morning that the statute was very clear, giving members of the House of Commons, during the session, and ministers of His Majesty at all times, during recess, as well, the privilege of franking their letters. My hon. friend relies upon the regulations of the department. Regulation 114 states that letters and other mailable matter sent out by public departments at Ottawa and franked as being departmental matter, enjoy the franking privilege. I explained, I think, and I call to my assistance the hon. gentleman who was long in the government

before my time, the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), what was the object of that regulation? It was enacted by the Post Office authorities at the time to prevent the civil servants, the officials of- various departments, from abusing the franking privilege, which appertains to the heads of the department and to the department itself. I do not want to take up time, but I stated this morning that it was found that officials were abusing the franking privilege, that they were franking letters for outside parties, and that is why the_ old government, with which my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) was formerly connected, enacted that regulation 114. I may say I had that confirmed by the deputy minister a moment ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am not aware that the plain words of this statute and of this regulation are to be interpreted upon any conjectural remarks of my hon. friend the Postmaster General.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I beg pardon.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I say I am not
aware that the words of the statute are to be interpreted upon any such conjecture as that offered by my hon. friend the Postmaster General. I take the words of the statute, and I shall repeat them again. The statute 'says that mailable matter may be sent out by the departments, and that matter so sent out by a department if it is to be carried free of postage must be departmental matter. I say so far as this letter is concerned, the department has absolutely denied that it did send it out as a department, and I say that every minister who has spoken on this matter has absolutely denied that this letter is of a departmental character. Then, I say the question falls. There is no more argument about it. There has been a persistent and plain violation of the statute and of the regulation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Let me put a question to my hon. friend. I ask him as a very eminent lawyer, would he say, putting his reputation at stake, that I as Postmaster General writing a letter to my son during recess could not frank that letter?

I will come to that. I was about to come to that when the Postmaster General asked the question. I say that under the strict terms of the stature and regulation, he has not that power, but in respect to trivial and casual matters of that kind no one in this House would think of raising any question. But it is not of that we are complaining. We are complaining of a system carried on deliberately from day to day and from week to week throughout the year by which the campaign literature of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House has been carried free of postage through the mails in Mr. LEMIEUX.
absolute violation of the law of this country. My hon, friend the Postmaster General, and my hon. friend the Solicitor General, ask if letters are to be opened. What a paltry argument that is. Of course, letters are not to be opened, not letters of a department or of members of parliament. But, when we have the clear and explicit declaration, of my hon. friend the Solicitor General that this practice is carried on systematically, day after day, week after week, and year after year, it does not come to a question of whether we shall open letters, but to a question whether this House shall or shall not pronounce its . condemnation of a systematic violation of the law of this country, concurred in, I am sorry to say, by the Postmaster General
There is really nothing further to say on the question, it seems to me. Where is my hon. friend to draw the line? He says that patent medicine advertisements cannot be sent out. If the Solicitor General were to persist in using his frank for such a purpose, and made a declaration on the floor of this House that he had done so in the past and intended to do so in the future, I presume my hon. friend the Postmaster General would feel compelled to take some steps in the matter. Again, I say, as between that and the literature that has been sent out, I can see absolutely no difference, so far as the interpretation of this statute and of this regulation is concerned. It is impossible to conceive that one can be within the statute and the other without the statute; they are exactly on the same plane. The statute, I again repeat demands that this franking privilege shall only be exercised by the department as such, and in respect of mailable matter of a departmental character, and as to both these characteristics my hon. friend the Postmaster General has admitted that the statute and regulation have not been complied with. I suggest, therefore, to the Postmaster General, with a view to correcting this evil and discharging that duty to the public which he undertook when he assumed the seals of office, that he should accept the resolution of my hon. friend from New Westminster, and put a stop to this practice which has been carried on during the past eight or ten years.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I desire to ask the hon. member (Mr. R. L. Borden) a question, not with a view to controversy, but for explanation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Certainly. .

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext:
The discussion is as to what is proper during the recess. The departments receive many letters-and this exemption includes letters sent to, as well as sent by, the department. Letters come addressed to the minister or to the department which may not be on departmen-

tal business at ail-they may be political letters. How are you going to deal with that? Is that ruled out under the section?	i	i

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: If they are not really on public business of a departmental character, they cannot properly come under the provisions of the statute. I know that awkward cases may be cited, possibly cases that are inconsistent with the usage established in the past. I am not concerned with that; I am taking the plain words of the statute, and the regulation. The minister (Mr. Paterson) has asked me a fair question and I desire to answer it fairly. Under the words of the statute, it seems to me, unless matter can be described as of a departmental character, and unless it is sent out by the department as such, it cannot go free in the mails. You cannot go further than that. But, as respects trifling and trivial instances, no one would think for a moment of raising any question. It is only when there is a ^regular, organized system of what I hold to be a violation of the Post Office law carried on by a department of the government, that the question is raised in this House. I think that the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) if he were satisfied that there was a violation of the law, would be as anxious as I am to see it brought to an end.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: I am not asking questions in a controversial spirit. But letters of all kinds oome to the departments. They might be letters on things which could not be called departmental. Would that be considered a violation of the law?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: As I have said, I think that the terms of the statute do not cover mail matter of that kind. But I say that such trifling instances are not worth talking about in this House. I am talking of the terms of the statute, and the regulations as I find them, and am giving what 1 sincerely believe to be the true interpretation.

Clearly, under the terms of the resolution itself, there is nothing before the House to justify the acceptance of the resolution, for it speaks merely of passing through the mail political matter under the frank of the Department of Justice, and there is no evidence of any such political matter having gone through the mail under the frank of the minister or of the department-there is only the trank of the Solicitor General, as admitted by himself. I think it is admitted on all sides that there is no limit to the right of a member to transmit and receive, free of postage, mailable matter during the session of the House, and any regulation made either by the Governor in Council or by the Postmaster General under authority o*f
the Postal Act limiting in any way the right of members to send mailable matter-regardless of whether that matter relates to politics or to anything else-is beyond the power of the Governor or the Post Office Department.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) thinks that ^ny member of the government who cites the practice of a government preceding the accession to office of the present government is endeavouring to take refuge behind something of which, apparently, he does not very much approve. But I think it is very material to this inquiry, and to all other inquiries of this kind to ascertain what has been the practice. I venture to say that it is unquestionably the fact that every minister of the government, from confederation down, has acted as though he, as a member of the government and head of a department, had in this matter, exactly the same right outside the session as a member of parliament has during the session. I say that the words of section 114 of the regulations do not limit that at all, but merely express what shall be accepted by the postal authorities as that which is to be accepted free of postage from the departments. From time immemorial what has come from a department under the frank of the head of the department is a matter in respect of which the Postal Department makes no inquiry, and I say that under this section there is no endeavour to limit that right-and if there were it would be ultra vires of the power of the government. There is nothing clearer than that the power to make regulations must be construed strictly, and that such powers cannot authorize prohibition. There is no power, under any regulation made under the Postal Act either by the Governor in Council or by the Postmaster General, to limit in any way the matter which may be transmitted and received either by a member of this House or Dy a department of the government. The practice has been -and it seems to me a sound and sensible practice-to recognize in the heads of departments the exact rights during recess which are claimed during session by the members of this House. The regulation, I think, can be very well read in that way. One can easily interpret section 114 not as limiting the class of mail matter which can be sent by any of the departments. It comes from the department, and goes through the post office, as a matter of course. I say there is nothing unreasonable in the practice, from confederation down to the present time, of a minister having the right to frank any matter which he chooses the same as a member of this House during the session. It seems to me there is great danger, in the case of certain members of this House, of their goodne3*

growing to plurisy. I do not think any thing can be more inconsistent than an endeavour to draw fine lines in regard to these matters. The Solicitor General referred to an instance of 1896. . It may not be amiss to refer also to something that occurred previous to the election of 1904. In consequence of the mailable matter which had accumulated-matter of a purely campaign character; the corridors of this building, as has been mentioned, having been filled with it-the threat was made that this House should be held up long enough to send that matter out, if the minister would not agree to send it out afterwards. And it was sent out after the House rose, and it took two special trains with mail clerks and a cost of thousands of dollars to send that political matter through the length and breadth of this country. It seems to me that when the mail matter is of one political complexion it meets with no objection from our friends of the opposition, but if it is of another political complexion then they deem it very objectionable to frank. It seems to me reasonable that ministers out of session should have the same right which members have in session, and I do not think that any other practice is possible. If you proceed to limit the character of the mail matter which a member may send out, you would have to hold an investigation into the character of the matter, an investigation which would certainly be most objectionable and undesirable. I think the same objection would apply to limiting ministers, and that is the reason why that interpretation of the Act has been followed since confederation.

Had the character of this communication that has been brought before the House, been at all in the line of decency, I presume there would have been very little said about it. But it is of such a character that every member of the government who has spoken about it has repudiated all knowledge of it, and the Solicitor General has repudiated having anything to do with it.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I never repudiated it.
The Solicitor General said that he knew nothing about the subject matter.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I said I did not read it all.
Did the Solicitor General read this article that he sent out?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Then I am correct in saying that he has repudiated having anything to do with the composition of this article.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean to say that he repudiates everything he does not read?

I have not sent out anything of this kind. But this is the point that I want to put before the House. A few years ago there was a great deal of campaign literature sent out by the Conservative party, and I sent out my share of it, but not one tithe of that literature ever reached its destination, owing to the refusal of the then Postmaster General to send it forward. That is what I rise to protest against. Not only did these gentlemen hold it up, but they actually robbed the mails, and I maintain that they left themselves open to criminal prosecution. They destroyed it by tons, I was going to say; at any rate, it was not sent forward, perhaps they sold it to raise funds for their own campaign literature. It was deliberately side-tracked, I purposely use the word ' deliberately,' it was side-tracked and destroyed. That was before the time of the present Postmaster General. I was informed that there were tons of that literature stored up in places here in Ottawa for some years after the elections were held. Now, when a person goes to the trouble of sending out respectable campaign literature, I think he has a right to require that it is conveyed to its destination. So far as the literature under discussion is concerned, I will not say anything except that the contents of the letter have been frankly repudiated by every respectable gentleman who has spoken on the matter to-day.

Reference has been made by the Postmaster General, and by the Solicitor General, and the member for Yukon (Mr. Congdon), to the state of affairs previous to the election of 1904; they stated that the corridors of the House were blocked by Conservative literature, and that two special trains had to be made up in order to take it forward. Let me inform you, Mr. Speaker, that the members of the Conservative party did prepare campaign literature previous to that election, they got it printed at Montreal, the envelopes were purchased there and addressed there, and each member paid his shaTe of the expense. The literature came up here by express, and the members had the privilege of franking it just as members of the government had. But how was it done by members of the government and their supporters? Every day during the session, in the Department of Agriculture, in the Department of the Interior and in the Department of Justice, there was a staff of civil servants employed in addressing this Liberal campaign literature, and it was going out by the cartload, blocking the mails every day so that we could not get ours off. But there was this difference. Their literature was paid for by the country, the civil servants of this country were engaged in addressing it, and I saw it

going out to the post office to be mailed, and the country paid for all that. But on our side we had to pay out of our own pockets all the expense, and when we tried to mail it we could not do so because the mails were blocked by the literature from the departments, the post office was blocked and was not able to receive our mail from the House of Commons. Those are the facts of the case. I was blamed for franking this literature. I franked a portion of it and sent it into some good Liberal constituencies. It was all moral literature, good religious literature.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I never blamed you.

But reference has been made to it here by other members. The fact is that the blocking of the mails was done by hon. gentlemen opposite in sending out their literature at the expense of the country, when they employed the civil servants to address it, while on our side we paid all the expense ourselves.

A few words with reference to the clause of the Act which is under consideration by the House, because I think I was Postmaster General when that Act was passed. The Act was passed for the purpose of limiting as far as possible the abuses that were practised by the too free use of the franking privilege. Every civil servant under the government had the franking privilege, and it was decided to limit that privilege, and the limitation is clearly set forth in the law. No minister has a right to frank any document except departmental documents during recess. Why should that not be so? What right has a minister of the Crown to a greater franking privilege than I have? We are alike members of parliament elected by our constituencies, and what right has a minister at any time of the year to send out to the electors campaign literature which I or any other member should not also have? Because I am in opposition am I to be debarred from doing it? That is the gravamen of the offence of which we complain. If we had the right, we would allow these gentlemen to do the same thing. But we have not the right, and we ought to be on a par with them as to our rights in this House. Therefore we insist upon the law being carried out. It is all very well for hon. members to make remarks upon the intention of parliament, but we are dealing with the statute as we find it, and we have no right to judge of the intentions of those who passed the Act. Here is the law, it is applied to us, and we cannot send out literature a day or two after the session is closed; we are debarred from sending it to our constituents. What we complain of is not that they send it out, but that they are taking a privilege which
the law does not give them, and which we are deprived of. Give us the same privilege as you have and we will make no complaints about it. All that we expect as representatives of the people is that we shall have the same right as you have. At present we have no rights during the recess. We insist upon our rights and that you shall not exercise a right which we are deprived of.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Many years ago when the government of Canada took over the administration of Indian affairs it was thought possible that the exclusive management should be carried on out of Indian funds, and for a number of years ait attempt was made to carry on the business in that way. The result was that the cost of management exceeded the yearly accruing revenue from the funds. The capital was being depleted by the cost of management, and if matters had gone on in that way the capital fund would have been exhausted. It was thought that that was not the proper way to carry on the business and at some period it was decided that the bulk of the cost of management should be voted out of the general treasury, and that the money taken from the capital funds of the Indians should be returned to that fund. So every year we have voted a certain amount as the. amount to be returned to that capital fund. I may say that at the rate we have been going the capital fund will soon be up to its original figure, and this charge will disappear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This vote is simply to replace, year by year, a certain portion of the money that was taken. The interest has been spent from year to year, as it was originally intended it. should be spent, but, instead of taking the shortage out of the capital, we ask parliament now to vote it, and not only so, but to make up the shortage that was created.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The two are of the same nature. There was a special fund provided by the province of Quebec, and there was a fund provided for the management outside of Quebec. speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

The increase in the Indian population is very slight. But (here are three hundred more officials than there were about fourteen years ago and the expense is greatly increased. A year or two ago the expenditure was $60,000 more than it had been a few years before that. Why should the expenditure increase in this way and the money be so extravagantly used?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend suggests that the expenditure is larger in proportion to the number of Indians than it was ten or twelve years ago. i have no doubt his statement is correct. The only answer

we can make is that we are giving a better service to the Indians than in times gone by. With the development of the country we have been able to take new areas under treaty, and to assume responsibilities in regard to them. We are carrying out those responsibilities, mainly in relation to education-school education, and education in farming and industry-to a greater extent than in former years. In doing that we think we have not only the sanction, but the cordial approval of the public.

I do not wish to enter upon a controversy now, but I am afraid the minister (Mr. Oliver) is not fully acquainted with the facts. For instance, up to two years ago there had been an increase, only one in tne number of school teachers in twelve years. If I had time I would like to show the condition of the Indian Department. I believe it is the duty of the Minister of the Interior to turn over the Department of Indian Affairs to some other minister who would have time to attend to it. I do not find so much fault with the minister. He has not only this Indian department to look after, but he has charge of immigration, public lands, homestead inspection, fire ranging and many other branches. It is impossible for one man to do alt this. Yet he retains the Indian Department, in the face of the fact that other ministers of the Crown are going around practically looking for something to do. It is no wonder that he has such cases as that of the St. Peter's reserve brought before this House. It is no wonder that charges are brought before this House such as I made two years ago, when I showed tnat out of 620,-0(K) acres of Indian lands, 500,000 acres had been sold at an upset price fixed by the department. That means nothing else than that the price was fixed by the deputy minister. And after the sample of work done by the deputy minister, I think it would be wise for the minister to take into consideration whether he is capable of handling the department, or if it is not time he should look about and get another man in his place. The minister speaks for the good work done for the Indians on educational lines. Does he want me to show the condition of the Indians in the United States and the splendid, uplifting work that is going on among the Indians of that country as compared with what is being done in Canada? The minister tells us that the Indians own $32,000,000 of property. Yet we find that there are 3,167 cases of tuberculous diseases. What is being done for them? And the physicians in charge of 41,000 Indians did not report at all-about half the physicians employed under the present deputy. I could take up hours of the time of this House with instances of this kind.
Mr, OLIVER.
Go on.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tolmie) would like to hear reasons for condemning the work of the Indian Department, I could give him facts to show that the department is carried on in a most careless, indifferent, and I might say, corrupt manner. The minister has had these matters called to his attention time and again. But, instead of taking hold of the department or allowing some other minister to do so, which I claim is his duty, he still continues to attempt the task, which is evidently beyond him, of managing all the affairs placed in his charge. I call the minister's attention to these matters as showing that the money is being recklessly spent.

I do not think the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) is warranted in making general assertions that money has been recklessly spent, and that the department is improperly and corruptly managed. These are easy things to say without attempting to bring evidence in support of them. I think I have some knowledge of the management of the Indian Department, at least in my riding. I happen to represent a district comprising nearly one-half the area of the province of Ontario, in which the greater portion of the Indian population of that province reside. And I am prepared to say that, in my judgment, the business of the Indians is well and honestly managed. I am prepared to say that there is a great improvement in the educational facilities afforded the Indians now over what there was even a few years ago. There are new buildings and new equipment, sanitary conditions are improved, and the position of the Indians generally improved. It is a very difficult thing to carry out the work efficiently, as it is there is an improvement upon the conditions of some years ago. Affairs are better managed than they were formerly. I am not finding fault with the past, but I think I have some knowledge of the matter, and my opinion is that there is a vast improvement on these lines.

I am satisfied the hon. gentleman (Mr. Conmee) is not acquainted with the matter at all. I went into the facts two years ago, and placed before the House statistics which went to show that out of 620,000 acres of land, tens of thousands of acres had been sold at ten cents and fifteen cents an acre, that dozens of islands had been sold at $1 apiece. Does the hon. minister call that taking care of the Indian lands of the country? I have a return covering every acre of land sold, showing where it was located and to whom it was sold. I could bring that return again and show page after page of records

of lands sold which even the hon. member (Mr. Conmee) would say were not sold at a right price. Why, in 1908, as I showed, there were some 3,000 Indians around James Bay who had not among them a single doctor or government official. There was a territory in Moosonee or Keewatin in which there were 10,000 Indians and not a government official amongst them. These are chlarges that have never been refuted, and that have been made time and again in this parliament.
These were not treaty Indians. They were not taken over by the department, and the government could hardly be held responsible for them.
But if the hon. gentleman will investigate Indian affairs, he will find that the department has spent tens of thousands of dollars on non-treaty Indians.

They were not treaty Indians at that time in the sense in which they are to-day. As to the sale of lands, the lands were sold for the market price at the time. All the Indian lands are sold, so far as I know, by public competition after advertisement. The hon. member shakes his head. I am well aware that Indian lands have been sold otherwise, but not of recent years. The hon. gentleman thinks he made very important charges against the Indian Department a couple of years ago. I venture to say that he has rot convinced anybody, in this House or out of it, that the charge was worth the paper it was written on, for the reason that the lands were sold at the market prices. I know of Indian lands settled by a previous administration on similar terms tc those applying to free grant lands in Ontario. I speak of the Manitoulin island. This was an Indian reserve. It was in the public interest that the land should be settled. The Indians to-day are better taken care of than they would have been if they had held it, because they have been furnished with industrial schools and industrial works, have been given an education and taught trades. The result is that they have advanced in intelligence and civilization to a very great extent as compared with ten or fifteen years ago. It is a very easy thing to find fault. I do not pretend to say that this department, or any other department, has not made mistakes, but I do say that it is unfair for the hon. member (Mr. Armstrong) to make such strong and sweeping charges as he has made without any evidence to back them up. Those charges are not true so far las Ontario is concerned.

According to the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Conmee's) own argument, he knows only very little of a small portion of this question of the Indians. He has not investigated the Indian report,
I venture to say he has not looked through it, yet he says that everything is going along smoothly. The hon. gentleman is the very man that will stand by this government in every bit of trickery and corruption that is carried on in the parliament of Canada. He stood up no doubt for the St. Peter's reserve. Does he really think that was a straight forward business-like transaction? Does he think that when the hon. member for Algoma (Mr. Boyce) brought up that charge last year In regard to Indian lands, does he think that also was a straight forward business-like transaction, and carried through for the benefit of the Indians? Then the sale of 620,000 acres I referred to. The hon. gentleman knows full well that those lands were not put up and disposed of by auction in a proper way, a large portion of those lands was disposed of either by private sale under the Indian agent, or at an upset price fixed by the department, that is to say, fixed by the deputy head.

The hon. gentleman is not justified in saying that I have not looked into the Indian reports. I do not profess to have examined all the Indian reports, but I have more or less knowledge of their contents. Now, the hon. gentleman said that the Indian lands referred to by the member for Algoma were sold at an upset price and without advertisement. What lands, and where?
I have a list of them, a stack of them several inches high.

Then the hon. gentleman refers to the St. Peter's reserve in the vicinity of Selkirk, and wants to know if I think T was justified in voting on that question as I did. I want to tell him that I do. In my opinion that was a businesslike transaction, carried out in the interest of the public and in the interest of the Indians themselves. I know the local conditions of Selkirk better than my hon. friend does, and I have no hesitation in saying that in my opinion that transaction was in the pubilc interest, and will be and is already proving to be in the interest of the Indian themselves. It is better for them to be away from the surroundings in which they were placed.
Why not then send them away in Ontario?

Well, I think they should be. I think that what the minister has done at Selkirk he should have done on the Rainy river. The condition of the Indians there is even worse, and the party to which my hon. friend belongs is responsible for it, and I will tell him why. In the days when the ownership of the territory was in dispute, when it became known that they were not to have control

7843
of the land, the Conservative government at Ottawa surveyed out a large number of reserves in that section of the country-
What has this to do with the item?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it is sufficiently relevant to the Indian land management to be allowed.

-which the Indians did not require, and upon which no Indian has yet settled. There is a large block of wild land reserves at the mouth of the. Rainy river, and there has never been a family of Indians on it to this day, and the whole country for nearly a hundred miles is cut up by several other reserves. Does the hon. gentleman say that that is in the public interest or in the interest of the Indians? I listened to the debate on the St. Peter's reserve, and I heard the arguments put up by hon. gentlemen opposite, and I was not convinced that that was not an honestly carried out transaction. It was absolutely necessary for the officials of the department to go there and act as they did act, if there was to be a surrender made. I heard nothing to convince me that there was any undue pressure brought upon the Indians to surrender their reserve. I believe they were left perfectly free to vote as they chose. There is no political object to be served by hon. gentlemen opposite in making these strong assertions. I was going to say ridiculous assertions, of dishonesty, corruption, deceit, wrong-doing, maladministration. It is easy for any one to make these charges, but my hon. friend is not building himself up, he is not advancing the reputation of his party in the country, but he is Tather pulling it down when he makes charges for which there is no foundation. The facilities afforded by this parliament for affording investigation are open to every member, and when he makes la charge of that character he has the means at his disposal of proving it. I think if I were sitting on the opposition side of the House, I would not be content with making assertions and reading a few affidavits extracted from Indians, drunk or sober; I would endeavour to furnish something better than that, I would avail myself of the machinery afforded by parliament to prove my charges or seek investigation otherwise.
Indians-Ontario and Quebec, general legal expenses, $13,500.
That seems to be a large sum of money to pay in legal expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amount is large, but it is the same amount as was voted last year. It is much larger than was formerly voted. The ordinary legal expenses which are incurred in the enforcement of law in Mr. CONMEE.
regard to reserves run to $3,000 or $4,000 a year. The reason this vote is so large is because we had to secure the settlement of the long outstanding and very celebrated Oka Indian case, in regard to a reserve on the Ottawa river. It perhaps would not be of advantage at this stage of the session to go into the details of the case, but it is a very celebrated question, and, some years ago, when matters had come to rather an acute stage it seemed to me that the best thing to be done was to get the case before the Privy Council, and get a final decision upon it, because no decision short of that would be final or acceptable to either parties to the dispute. We have, 'therefore, instituted proceedings and will carry the case to the Privy Council, and $10,000 of this amount is. in regard to the Oka Indians case. There has been one decision. The first decision has been handed down by the court at Montreal and proceedings are now being taken to have the case carried to the court of appeal from which it will be carried to the Privy Council, and we hope to get a final settlement of the question.

The small band of Indians in the riding I represent are interested in some degree with regard to the Oka Indians. I do not know whether their phase of the dispute comes under the case that will be submitted to the Privy Council, or whether a final settlement has been made as to what their rights are. I think their claim had something to do with timber. I would like to know what is the position of this band in regard to the Oka dispute. Requests have been made to me from time to time to look into the matter, but I have found it difficult to ascertain the exact position. I shall not take up the time of the committee now, but I will make private inquiries in the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The settlement in my hon. friend's constituency of some of the Oka Indians is the result of an effort which was made to settle this difficulty, and some years ago an arrangement was. entered , into whereby it was hoped that the Indians, who were contesting for the ownership of the reserve at Oka, would take land in the towmship of Gibson. Some of them agreed to do so, but others refused to move, and it is in regard to the settlement of the land rights of those who remained that the aase has been entered. Those who removed to the township of Gibson did so with the understanding that they exchanged their land rights in Oka for the land rights which they secured in Gibson, but their right to a share of the band fund still remains. They are entitled to a share in the fund of the Oka band, and as a matter of fact do now receive their share. They are debit with otherwise the same as other Indians. There may be some other matter in dispute

that they .are not satisfied with, but that is the principle one upon which we are dealing with them.
I understand that they are not receiving any money in a general way like the other tribes. I do not know what the minister means when he says that they do receive their money.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They are not receiving any cash. The fund of the band is very small, and there are certain expenses which are taken out of that fund for the benefit of the two separated sections of the band- those at Oka, and those at Gibson. They are dealt with, in so far as the funds are concerned, on just the same footing as those of Oka. The Auditor General's Report for 1908-9, at plage 116-1, shows that they have a balance at their credit of $4,835.32. That is their capital, and of course the interest on that is spent from time to time for the necessities that arise. It is a very small amount.
Indians-Nova Scotia-repairs to roads and dyking, $450.
There is an increase.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is for improving roads that .pass through the Indian reserves, and the work is done on the reserves.
Is that work done by the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

I would like to ask the minister whether in some cases this is taken out of the Indian fund or is always a grant from the government. I suppose that some of these Indian bands are quite wealthy, and that they have plenty of money to make their own roads. Last year a sale was made of the timber upon the reserve on the French river, and the proceeds ran up to somewhere over a million dollars. The average Indian will be much wealthier there than the average white man, and some discrimination should be made under these circumstances with regard to road making. The wealthy Indians should make their own roads while the poor ones should be taken care of to some extent.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Where a band has a fund which can be used for this purpose the fund is used, but in this case this band had no fund, or whatever fund it has is so _ very limited that it would be simply using it up. We, therefore, have to give these Indians money for improvements or the improvements cannot be undertaken. It is not considered to be in the public interest that a road, where it passes through
an Indian reserve, should be in an impassable condition.
You allow them to earn the money by doing the work?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

On one side of the Kettlepoint Indian reserve is the village, and on the other side is a farming district, and for the last two or three years the road around the lake in the reserve has been impassible and a long detour has to be made to get to the other side. 'There is a summer resort at the reserve also, and I hope the minister will repair that road.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
A note will be taken of what the hon. gentleman said, and ive will look after it.

There is an increase of $500.

speechtext: That provides for an increase in the salaries of the three superintendents in New Brunswick as follows: R. A. Irving, from $500 to $800; James White, from $350 to $450; and G. E. Baxter, from $250 to $350. The explanation is that we do not think that the salaries have been reasonable for the time taken in connection with the work.
How many Indians are there in New Brunswick?
