Indians-salaries, relief aud seed grain,
medical attendance,	-Prince Edward Island, $1,650.
How many Indians are there in Prince Edward Island?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Were there Indians down there originally?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, their reserve is on an island off the mainland; Lennox island.
Wharf - Lennox island, Prince Edward Island, $2,500.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Indians there have to communicate with the mainland to sell their produce. The old wharf has gone out of value, and thi3 is part payment of the cost of a new wharf, the other part being put up by the Department of Public Works.
Does this complete it?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Are these Indians farming on their lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, they farm, but in a small way.
Are any efforts being put forth to make good citizens of them, to induce them to take up their lands separately?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think so. The effort of the department has been to improve their condition as Indians, that is to say, to induce them to cultivate their land and to become self-supporting.
Are they nearly selfsustaining?	~

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, these people are.

It seems to me that the efforts of the Indian Department ought to be directed along that channel. If we are ever going to assimilate the Indian population, it will have to be done in that way. I do not think the case is hopelesst1 I might cite the case of a band of Oka Indians that went to the Tiding I represent. These Indians have their lands and they farm almost as successfully .as the average white man. They are no burden on the community, and many of them are examples of what might be done with the Indians. I think a great many of the Indians would become good citizens of Canada with a little time and attention.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know that it would be profitable to argue out that question just now. It is a very, very broad question. I merely stated what has been the policy of the department. These Indians cultivate in severalty and they own their land in community. As Indians, they have certain privileges. My hon. friend has placed before the House the suggestion that the Indians have less advantages than the_white men. The Indian believes that Mr. OLIVER.
by the terms of the treaty with him he has advantages over the condition of the white citizen, and it would not be merely a matter of getting the Indian to support himself, in which we have been successful, in a large number of cases, but of getting him to give up the special privileges, advantages and exemptions which he has as an Indian and which he would lo3e if he became a citizen.

It seems to me that the experiment might well be tried in Prince Edward Island.
Indians - Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories-annuities and commutations, $172,000.
There is a decrease hers of $1,200. Is that due to a decrease in the number of Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It does not necessarily indicate a decrease in the number. There are commutations, and there are also failures to apply for annuities. We make the calculation that each year on these figures as well as on the number of Indians.
Indians-Manitoba, etc.-Live stock, $6,960.
How are these animals purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The principal purchasers here are of bulls, which we buy at the thoroughbred sales if enough are offered, and, if not, we have to buy otherwise. The oxen and the other stock we buy locally.
Do you supply them with this much each year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; the amount is the
same as last year.
Why is it necessary to continue this annually?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is necessary, of course, constantly to bring in new blood. We are not restocking every reserve every year, but, because of the large number of reserves which must be supplied, we have to continually make purchases of stock.
Was the full amount spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What did the Indians do with these males? Did they kili them and eat them?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They employed them as other stock raisers do.
They are bought by the government. Do the Indians appropriate them as their own?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, subject to government supervision. Of course, the effect is ultimately to make the Indians, as my hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Wright)

-suggested, self-supporting. So we furnish them from time to time with stock, and supervise them in the rearing and disposition of these animals.
Indians, Manitoba, Ac.-Supplies for destitute Indians, $121,105.

I understood the minister to say before six o'clock that all the supplies for these reserves in western Canada are purchased by tender. I notice the names of a great many firms from eastern Canada sending out supplies to the west, and I was wondering how, if bought by tender, these people in eastern cities could supply the material cheaper than those in the west, considering the high freight rates.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The freight has to be paid whether the dealer lives in the west or in the east. Of course, in asking for bids we ask every one, and take the lowest bidder wherever he may live. The price is the priee^ of the goods delivered, so it makes no difference to us whether the dealer is in the west, or in the east.
Indians, Manitoba, Ac.-Hospitals, medical attendance, medicines, Ac., $c2,057.
The minister may now be able to answer the question I put to him a few moments ago: Who is the medical attendant at Swan Lake?
Cooper.
How long has he been acting in that capacity, and what remuneration does he get?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has been medical attendant for some time, I cannot say when he was appointed. He gets a retainer of $60 a year, and then he is paid for each trip he makes to the reserve.
How much did he draw last year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not that information for last year. Of course, the Auditor's report contains the amount for the year before last.

The minister's department lias. no doubt been advised of the poisoning case that took place on that reserve. There was a great deal of correspondence in the press regarding it last summer, and there was a difference of opinion as to how it should have been dealt with. Possibly the- minister or his deputy could tell us about the lines of action the government took with regard to it. I remember there were certain citizens there who thought the government did not do its duty, and I would like to know what effort they made to discover the cause of the poisoning, or whether they attempted to prosecute those who had been giving, I think, some kind of medi-246
cine with an extract of peppermint in it. I know the people in that locality thought the government were very inactive, and should have followed it up a little closer.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think it would be better for my hon. friend to allow the matter to rest, and I will look into it. It is rather a serious question, and I will give him the information at a later date.	-
In what form will he give it to me?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Probably we will not be through with our estimates to-night, and there are moreover some supplementaries coming, and there' will be another occasion when I can give the hon. gentleman the information across the floor, or by laying the papers on the table.

There was formerly an
Indian hospital on the reserve near Ross-burn, and I understand that hospital has been closed, or removed to the town of Birtle. I would like the minister to explain on whose recommendation that was removed, or why it was removed from Ros-thern reserve. Is there any local difficulty there?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It was thought the hospital at Rossbum was not as conveniently located for administration as it would be at Birtle. Birtle is an important railroad point, with good railway facilities that did not exist at Rossbum. The hospital was removed on the report of the inspector, Mr. Swinford.

I notice an item in the Auditor General's Report for preventing the spread of tuberculosis among the Indians. What steps do the government take to prevent the spread of that disease amongst the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend understands that it is only in recent years that the subject of tuberculosis has been taken up seriously. But the department has taken it up seriously within the last few years, and this vote is for the purpose of affording assistance. Treatment is given to special cases, that is to say, provision is made for the removal of certain cases to places where the patients may get better treatment. We have established tent hospitals at several points, and generally speaking, we are taking cognizance of tuberculosis amongst the Indians with a view of keeping abreast with the advance of medical knowledge.
I see you give a grant to the Toronto tuberculosis hospital; has that anything to do with the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is a grant made to the Toronto hospital by the Indian Department, there are several Indian child-



ren in that hospital now, and it is in connection with these and similar cases that this vote is asked for.
Indians-Man., &c.-Triennial clothing, treaties 4 and 7 and adhesion to treaty 5, $2,700.
Where are these goods purchased, and how?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The clothing is made at the Kingston penitentiary and purchased from the penitentiary authorities.
Why did the government have to give each one of the Indians so much land on the St. Peter's reserve, when they got them to surrender that reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In severalty?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The reason was that these Indians, at the time of the transfer from the Hudson Bay Company, were occupants in severalty of their land and were, in law, original settlers of the province of Manitoba. They afterwards decided to become treaty Indians and were given the reserve as treaty Indians. We were anxious to secure the surrender of their reserve and their removal to another reserve, and it was desired, too, at the same time that we were wiping out their rights as Indians in that reserve, to also wipe out such rights as they might have as original settlers of Manitoba at the time of the transfer. For that purpose that provision was embodied in the deed of surrender. When each Indian got his patent the receipt that he signed was a receipt, not only for the land, but it was a receipt which stated that it was in full of his rights as an original settler of the province of Manitoba.
Is that the only case we have in the west?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no other case.
Is the minister lrivirm any success in inducing the Indians to surrender the balance of the Swan lake reserve, and what effort is being made by the government in that direction?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We were successful in getting the surrender of a portion of the Swan lake reserve a year or two ago. We have settled with them and disposed of the land, but we did not think it was wise or likely to be successful to go right back immediately for a further surrender. We thought it was better to clean up the arrangement that had been made, and then after that had been done we could go back and see if the Indians would be willing to surrender a further amount, which we are quite prepared to do.

The minister stated that he thought it was better to make a clean up of that which had already been under-Mr. OLIVER.
taken. It has been cleaned up, I understand, very successfully, not only to the Indians themselves, but to the people of that particular district. I would suggest that the minister now try and get, at least, a large portion of the reserve surrendered and brought under cultivation. While the minister has stated that he had succeeded in getting a portion of it, there is another portion that it would be a great deal more desirable to get the surrender of. I can assure him that the citizens of that section will appreciate it very much if the minister will begin negotiations along careful lines and try to get the balance of that reserve surrendered. It is not necessary that I should go into the reasons why it should be surrendered more than to say that it lies between the town of Swan Lake on the east and the town of Marieopolis on the west. It is the best agricultural land, and it is simply lying idle there. It is a great injury to the development of these towns and the district in general. I hope the minister will begin negotiations right along the same lines as those which proved so successful before. I can assure him that if he succeeds as he did before the people will appreciate it very much.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will be very glad to take up the matter at the earliest possible opportunity.
How many Indians are there still on the Swan lake reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: While we were successful in securing the first surrender it does not necessarily follow that we will be successful in making the second attempt. My hon. friend may have heard of the man who was successful in getting away with the mill, but was caught when he came back for the dam.

I might draw the minister's attention also to the Long Plain reserve, which lies between Portage la Prairie and the Assiniboine. A great many people have asked me to bring it to the attention of the minister in order that he might try to get a surrender of a portion of it, at least, if not all. There was a time when this was not considered valuable land from the fact that it was well wooded, but fires have been doing their work, settlers have been cleaning up the land, and it is now practically clean land. It could be very easily brought under cultivation, and it is adjacent to good settlements- Indian Ford settlement across the river and Portage la Prairie plains to the north- and if the minister would enter upon negotiations, I think this would be a favourable time to secure the surrender.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I will be very glad to take a note of it. There are 113 Indians on the Swan lake reserve.

Indians-Man., &c.-Sioux, $4,498.
There is a decrease of half.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is on account of some mill machinery which we furnished last year and which we are not furnishing this year.
How many Indians are there on the Turtle mountain reserve, and how much land have they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are 15 at the Turtle mountain reserve, and it is one square mile in area. There has been a surrender taken of part of the reserve.
Indians-Man., Ac.-grist and saw-mills, $4,037.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We got the Indians to surrender the reserve west of Battleford and take a reserve north of the river and one of the terms was that we should provide them with milling machinery.
^Indians-Man., Ac.- general expenses, $230,-

Dr. Lafferty is the
medical officer attending Blackfoot reserve and he is certainly a very excellent physician, but he lives at Calgary which is quite a distance from the reserve. Dr. Lafferty draws $600 a year for this service, and 1 would like to know from the minister in what way he is able to attend to his duties on the reserve and earn this money?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He makes regular visits once a month and is subject to call in emergency.
Is there any other doctor attached to that reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is Dr. Rose, who is in attendance on the hospital on the reserve.

Dr. Rose lives at Gleichen. If Dr. Lafferty were living near this reserve I would have nothing to say. because he is an excellent doctor. But, Dr. Lafferty lives 55 miles away. The minister says he makes one trip'a month to the reserve and I find he has received $45.60 for railway fares which I presume is between Gleichen and Calgary. That would represent about 20 trips. His salary of $600 a year would therefore be at the rate of about $30 a trip. I do not mind that so much as the fact that it is against my principle to have a doctor residing at such a distance from the scene of his labours. For instance, none of us would have our family physician in the city of Toronto when we could find medical men to attend us in Ottawa. Dr. Rose, and at least one other doctor lives in Gleichen, and in the interest of effective medical service to the Indians we should, I think have their medical attendant living near them.
249*
That is the point I bring to the attention of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Dr. Rose attends the church hospital on the Blackfoot reserve towards the support of which we pay $1,-2^2, so that we think we are doing something towards medical attendance for the Indians. It is true Dr. Lafferty lives at Calgary, and that he is only called upon to make 12 visits a year in addition to emergency calls, and it is true that there could be very much more convenient medical attendance given by Dr. Rose or by one of the medical men living at Gleichen. But there is always a variety of opinion as to the value of the services of medical men, and the old saying is that doctors differ. In administering the affairs of a reserve having about 800 Indians it is not out of place, and not a waste of public money, and not to the disadvantage of the Indians that we should have making monthly visits to that reserve and ready for emergent calls a gentleman of the admittedly high qualifications of Dr. Lafferty. I suppose my hon. friend (Mr. Magrath) will admit that he has probably considerably higher qualifications than have the gentlemen who are resident in Gleichen. It is a matter of opinion as to which is the best way to serve the Indians, and up to the present time we have taken the view that the_ interests of the Indians and of the public are best served by securing the somewhat eminent services of Dr. Lafferty in conjunction with the hospital attendance of Dr. Rose.

I agree with the minister that doctors differ. Dr. Lafferty is a very capable physician, and the same may be said of the gentlemen who are practis-, ing in Gleichen. Dr. Lafferty also attends the Stony reserve. I would like to know at what point on the railway west of Calgary he has to go to get to the reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The station that people generally go to when they are visiting the Stony reserve is Alorley, 'and I think "it is in the neighbourhood of some 50 miles from Calgary.

I do not entertain the same views as the minister with regard to this matter, and I suppose there is no use my pressing the subject further. I don't mind Dr. Lafferty going to the Blackfoot reserve or to the other reserve either so long as the Indians get proper medical attention. but my view is that the medical men at Gleichen should attend to the Indians who are located on the reserve near by. May I ask the minister what results if any have been obtained in dealing with the blood Indians in respect to releasing a portion of their reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There have been a number of attempts made, but without success,

to secure the surrender of a portion of the Blood Reserve. Last fall I visited the reserve to discuss matters with the Indians, and while I did not think it advisable to discuss the question of surrender with the Indians, I found them very strongly against the idea. I would think that the prospect of securing a surrender there is rather remote. Last year we secured a surrender of a portion of the Piegan reserve, and we have some hopes that as a result of that surrender when its terms have been carried out and the Indians realize the benefits that will accrue to them from it, the Bloods will be influenced to follow the example of the Piegans. The Bloods, Piegans, Sarcees and Blackfeet were allied tribes and -whatever interests one tribe interests the other. We thought that having broken the circle and secured the surrender of a part of one reserve, it was better policy to wait until the results of that surrender had made themselves apparent before we approached the other bands definitely with a proposal for a surrender. My hon. friend is aware that strong efforts were made to prevent the Piegan surrender going through; misrepresentations were made in regard to it and the efforts of the department were hampered in a great degree. This being the case we thought it was better that the action taken by the department should speak for itself, and we have hopes that when that has taken place we will have results in the cases of some of the other reserves.

My opinion is that it would be better in the interest of the Indian if we were to take a perpetual lease from him instead of giving a fee simple title, that is that the Indians lands should be sold carrying a perpetual mortgage. For instance, the Canadian Pacific railway irrigated lands carry a perpetual mortgage of 50 cents an acre. If you go to the Indians and say:	We do not want to take
the title from you, and offer him a rental based on 6 per cent interest on say, for the purposes of this- argument, a sale price of $16.66 an acre, it would be equivalent to $1 an acre a year. I think if a proposal of that kind were put before the Indian wherein the land was retained as security for the interest or rent, and that as long as the purchaser or his assignee paid the $1 per acre per year, the occupant would have the use of the land, such a proposal it appears to me would appeal to the Indian. It is possible to sell lands in that way because the Canadian Pacific railway have been very successful in selling their irrigated lands on those terms. As I understand you can sell the land and the Indian can claim 50 per cent of the purchase money. The other 50 per cent the government holds and pay the Indian three per cent on it, whether the rate at which the government Mr. OLIVER.
can borrow money abroad goes up or djvn. That rental method is successful to-day in the disposal of -western lands and it could be applied to these Indian lands.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is a very broad question, and I would not like to bring on a lengthy discussion, but the 50 cents an acre on the Canadian Pacific railway irrigated lands is an insurance guaranteeing a water supply for the crops when water is needed. There is no such insurance in the case of the Indian lands, and while many men would be willing to pay a rental of 50 cents an acre to secure a water supply in a country that may be subject to lack of rainfull they would hesitate to pay a dollar or fifty cents an acre interest when there was no such insurance connected with it. The idea of a tenant proprietorship in the Northwest does not appeal to me. The policy of the government is to have a population on the land who shall be the owners in fee simple of that land, and any proposal, no matter how attractive, that would involve tenancy rather than proprietorship, viewed from the standpoint of the best interests of Canada and the west, would not appeal to my mind.

It is an absolute ownership as long as the rent is paid. I have discussed this with prominent real estate men who are largely engaged in settling the west, and they have said they could sell the whole Blood reserve if they had an opportunity to do so on that basis.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend speaks of real estate men who are settling the west. The business of the real estate man is not the settlement of the west, but the holding up of the settler of the west.
It is another case in which the hon. gentleman and myself differ, and we are too near the end of the session to take up any time discussing it.

How are things progressing at the Piegan agency with reference to the winding up of that sale? T understand the sale is completed, and I am prepared to admit that the selling of the land is popular with the people of that country, and that there is no complaint in connection with the sale. There was complaint with regard to the consent of the Indians; it was claimed that there was dissatisfaction when the land was sold.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The total area of the reserve was 116,096 acres. There was surrendered for sale 22,338 acres. There were actually sold 12,000 acres and the sum realized was $205,692. The amount immediately available for expenditure on behalf of the Indians was $54,564. There were 471 souls in the band. We propose to invest this $54,000, that was immediately available, in machinery and implements for the benefit

of the band to enable them to go on with the work of breaking up their reserve, cultivating it, and making it productive. Among the implements we propose to buy are a 36 horse-power traction steam engine, to cost $4,046; a Oockshutt gang plough, 30 sets double harness, 6 seed drillers; 4 binders, and a number of other implements. There will be five and a half miles of fencing, and an engineer will be employed at a salary of $125 a month to have charge of the land breaking work.
How many months in the year will he be engaged?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say at the moment. I may explain the purpose of the traction engine. Most of my hon. friends are aware that a great deal of the land in southern Alberta is being broken up by the aid of engines instead of by horses, and we have found by our experience on the Blood reserve that it is economical, and advantageous to invest in such an engine for the purpose of breaking up the land.

I understand that the franchise was extended to the Indians in this district under certain conditions embodied in the order in council passed last June, by which if they take out patents for a certain portion of land, and put it under cultivation, &c., they will be eligible to vote. I want to know if they are taking advantage of the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is a provision in the Indian Act whereby on proclamation being issued in regard to any band, the members of that band are entitled on the fulfilment of certain conditions set forth in the Act to be enfranchised. But the conditions surrounding the enfranchisement are such that they are very seldom taken advantage of in any part of Canada, and so far as we are aware they are not taken advantage of to any degree up to the present time in the west. However, the privilege is there if the Indian wishes to become enfranchised; he may become, to all intents and purposes, a white man if he wants to, but he does not want to.

This is a new undertaking in regard to these Indian reserves. After listening to the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Herron), and to what the minister has said, it seems to me we have a fairly good way of bringing those other reserves under cultivation. For instance take Swan lake. There it would be easy to bring the land under cultivation, and if it were made to produce, the citizens of the towns mentioned a while ago, would get the benefit. I would make a strong plea to have that land brought under cultivation. The gasoline or steam engine has worked for the good of the Indian on the reserve mentioned, and also on that section
of land down in the Indian ford district. If the government is going to undertake a policy of that kind. I would put in a claim to have the lands in the county I represent cultivated as much as the Blood Indian reserve or any other reserve in Alberta. I am not finding any fault with what has been done up there,
I simply want to impress upon the minister the great benefit to these communities I have mentioned, if the land were brought under cultivation.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend has rather a wrong idea in this connection. What was done m regard to the Piegan reserve was done to meet the views of the Indians, and we are prepared to meet those views in that way when those views are expressed. But we cannot compel them to adopt these views.
It would be a good thing to suggest to them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but unless the people have the idea themselves, it is very possible that the suggestion would not work out. In the case of the Piegans, they had seen that the Bloods had succeeded in getting a large area of land broken up, and that they were becoming very prosperous and independent by reason of that cultivation. Then they did not have sufficient machinery to break up the land, but they believed that if they could get the land broken up they could work it to advantage. So it was the possibility of securing this machinery to enable them to bring their land under cultivation, that induced them to part with a portion of their reserve. It was not the money they were going to get; it was the fact that they would be enabled to employ their energy to advantage, and profit by bringing under cultivation the soil of the remaining part of the reserve.
Indians-British Columbia-salaries, $28,520.
Has Mr. Vowell resigned?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He has resigned, but his resignation takes effect only at the end of the present fiscal year.
Has the department taken steps towards the appointment of his successor?	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No steps have been taken yet.
Have no applications been made for the office?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I could not say that there have or have not been. We have not been considering applications up to this time, as the resignation does not take effect until March 31 next.

Although it does not directly bear on this item, I would like to ask whether or not there has been a sale either effected or in contemplation of the Kapilano reserve, situated within the cjr-poration limits of the city of Vancouver?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No sale has been made, nor is any at present in contemplation.
I am very glad to hear it. Is the department likely to consider an offer to purchase that reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As my hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) is aware, the condition of title in regard to reserves in the province of British	Columbia	is	such,	at the	present time, that it does not seem to us to	be wise	or	good	public	policy for us to enter upon any negotiations for the alienation of title. We do not think that tlie interest of the Indians would be served by an attempt to pass title at the present time when we are not in a position to give a clear title. The subject has been matter for discussion between an officer of the British Columbia government and the Justice Department during the past few days. I am afraid that we may not be able to reach a conclusion in regard to it without a reference to the Privy Council. But, for the present, we do not feel that we would be justified in undertaking to deal with this question of Indian lands when the question of title is in its present condition.

In any event, I suppose, the minister would take the view that this Kapilano reserve, situated as it is within the corporation limits of the city of Vancouver, might better be sold to the public than to a private person. The minister knows the situation of that reserve. I am glad to know that he is not contemplating any sale of it to a private purchaser. I rather think there is a very strong feeling there that, if that reserve is alienated at all, it should be alienated to the city of Vancouver, in the heart of which it lies.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the disadvantage of having that and other reserves in the vicinity of Vancouver remain where they are, and I will be very glad to take any steps possible to secure the change of title, that is, to have the Indians removed and make this land available for the expansion of the city's development. And, as soon as the question of title can be settled, if the responsibility remains with us, I can assure my hon. friend, no time will be lost in trying to bring the matter to a point that will enable this land to be used-to bring it under taxation and in process of development. As to the disposing of it specially to the city, I would not like to give any definite pledge on that point. My hon. friend will under-Mr. OLIVER.
stand that, as administering Indian affairs, our business is to secure the best value possible for the Indians. All I can say is that, if it should fall to us to have the administration of that reserve, and to have the right to give a clear title, I would be as glad to sell it to the city as to anybody else, provided the city would pay for it. But, our interest, as administering Indian affairs, would be to get as much as possible for the land.	_
You could cut it up and sell it by auction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Cowan) can rest assured of this-that there will be no private disposition of it.

I am very glad to have that assurance. I think the minister expressed in the fall of 1908, by way of telegram, his feeling as Minister of the Interior, that this government would release to the city of Vancouver its title to the Indian reserve provided the provincial government would do the same, and the Indians were settled with. I think the minister will remember that in October, 1908, a telegram was sent from him to Mr. Mac-Innes, who was then a candidate for Dominion honours. And I would like to be assured that that still is his policy. Let me give the reason why we should still have that assurance. The city of Vancouver has rested with a good deal of faith on the assurance contained in that telegram, in the faith that the reserve will finally become the property of the city, provided, as the minister says, that they deal as generously as anybody else with the Indians, and provided they get whatever reversionary interest the province may have. They have rested upon that. We have rested upon that, and have been pursuing a course with the object of procuring that property, relying upon that telegram the minister sent in October, 1908. I wish to know if the minister still holds the view expressed in that telegram, and whether the city is still justified in holding the hope of procuring the title in the city to that reserve, provided, as the minister says, that the city will settle in a generous way with the Indians.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would not like to bind myself to the wording of the telegram unless I saw it, and I do not just remember now what was in it. But if the position which I stated to the House to-night accords with that of the telegram; I know what I said to-night, and I am willing to stand by that. Our policy is, as I stated at some length the other night, that where the value of the land is worth more to the Indian than the land itself, we exchange the land for the money. In order to do that to the advantage of the

Indian, of course there must be a possibility of giving a clear title, and that being done, then the land goes to the man that will pay the most for it.

In this case I can remind the minister what was in that telegram, and I think he will recall it to his memory. It was a telegram to M*. Me-Innis saying that the Dominion would convey to the city the Kapilano reserve, provided the city made a settlement with the Indian and procured a release of the reversionary interest of the province

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I would have to supplement that by saying that the terms to the Indians would have to be satisfactory to the department as well as to the Indians.
That is what that telegram meant. The minister will note that really he gives the city of Vancouver a refusal of that Indian reserve.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it gives them an opportunity to bid upon it, but they would have to bid higher than anybody else in order to get it.
Indian education, $480,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are building a new school house on the Oneida reserve, $3,000; another on the Caughnawaga reserve, $6,500; and we are building a boarding school in the Yukon for which we are asking $20,000. These are items of increase over last year.
What about the industrial schools at Elkhorn and Regina, have these been abolished?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have had a great deal of discussion with the Teligious- bodies who are conducting boarding and industrial schools, with a view to a readjustment of the burden which some of them are finding rather heavy. There was an understanding, as we thought, by whjcli the Elkhorn school would be closed, but the understanding was not carried out, and that school remains in the position it was in before. The school at Regina, however, has been closed, in accordance with an understanding we arrived at with the Presbyterians who were managing the schooi at Regina. On an understanding with them, we closed the Regina school because it was not well situated for carrying on the work. We put up a boarding school on the File Hills reserve, and increased the amount per head at all the Presbyterian boarding schools in Saskatchewan from $72 to $100. That is the arrangement made with the Presbyterian church, with which they are satisfied.
Indian education-to provide a further amount for buildings and per capita grant for residential schools, $122,010.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This is in regard to boarding school. I will give the list.
To increase the per capita grant and the number of pupils at the Fort William orphanage, Fort William, Ontario, $2,000.
This is for the purpose of recognizing the character of the building that has been erected there. It is an absolutely modern building in every particular, and we think it is right and proper that where any church, out of its own resources, provides the capital for a first-class building such as this we should give the maximum grant. This mission was not receiving the maximum grant under the conditions of the old building, but when they got into their new building we considered that they were entitled to the maximum.
To provide an amount for the erection of an addition to File Hills boarding school, $15,000.
This is the proposition that I mentioned a few minutes ago in connection with the Presbyterian church.
To provide for an increase of ten pupils each for the Wabiscow and Whitefish Lake Church of England boarding schools, $1,440.
To provide a per capita grant for ten additional pupils at the Sturgeon Lake Roman Catholic boarding school, $720.
To provide for the erection of a Church of England boarding school on the Blackfoot reserve, $20,000.
The church of England had a boarding school on the Blackfoot reserve. The building had been erected by _ themselves, but it became unsanitary and it was decided to close it up. They were not able to replace it, and we thought that in this case the government would be warranted, in order to provide for the education of the Indians, in providing this sum.
To provide a grant for forty pupils at $72. $2,880.
We are erecting the building, and therefore, we do not give the maximum grant with respect to the pupils.
To provide for the erection of buildings for the Kootenay Indian Industrial school, $60,000.
This is a very large boarding school at St. Eugene in the Kootenay country near Fort Steele. It is an old established school, it has done a great deal of work, but the buildings have become absolutely unsanitary. We think it is right that a good building should be put up.
To erect new building for the Alert Bay Girls1 Home and provide equipment, $20,000.
Making a total of $122,040. This is an increase in the pupilage and per capita

grant in some cases, and it makes provision for new, substantial and sanitary buildings. '
Post office, outside service-salaries and allowances, $3,169,028.50.

Would the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) be good enough to tell us why he removed the post office at Dickson, Ontario, from the place where it formerly was, and what reason he has to give in view of the fact that he has received a number of communications, petitions and affidavits urging upon him the necessity of allowing the post office to remain where it is, and would he at the same time tell the committee why it is not possible for him to return that post office to the locality in which it was formerly situated?	_

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I inquired as to the facts of this case at the request of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong), and I found that some time ago the postmaster at Dickson in the united counties of Stormont and Cornwall left the province of Ontario to settle in Saskatchewan. After he left there were two applications to locate the post office at two different sites, and the inspector selected a site at a distance of about one mile and a quarter from the former location. He would have selected the place formerly occupied by the ex-postmaster were it not that a station had been opened on the Ottawa and New York railway near which we were obliged to open a new post office, and to equalize the distance we had to locate this one a little further west. Since my attention has been called to the matter I have asked the deputy minister to inform me whether there was enough population at the site of the former post office to justify the erection of a new one there, so as to satisfy the community I expect to have the report shortly, and if there is room for another post office there I will open one with pleasure.
Has a post office inspector been appointed at North Bay ?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Limoges who is well known to my hon. friend (Mr. Gordon) was appointed two or three months ago, but before entering on his duties we put him under the direction of the post office inspector at Ottawa. I understand that Mr. Limoges, whom I have met, is a very able man and has resided in the district for a great many years. I believe he will prove satisfactory to the department and to the public. I may tell my hon. friend that a few days ago we selected a young man of great ability, who has been in the service for many years, as assistant inspector to Mr. Limoges. I refer to Mr. Ross, son of the general superintendent of'

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: post offices in the Dominion, and who, I believe will give as much satisfaction to the public in that district as his father has given throughout the Dominion.
I thought an inspector had to be in the service of the Post Office Department for a certain period before being appointed.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We can appoint an inspector who has not been in the service, but the assistant inspector must have been at least 5 years in the service.
That is a curious way of doing business. It would seem to be common sense that the inspector is the man who should have more knowledge than the assistant inspector.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: That is the law as I found it.
Is that a proper business way of conducting affairs ?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: In the larger cities we appoint as postmasters, men who have been in business and are well known to the general public, and then we give them as assistants the best men we have in the service.
You don't depend much on your inspectors.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: On the contrary. The inspector before assuming his duties, has to undergo a period of training. Of course, we select men of tact and ability and men who know the district, and in a short time they can become efficient officers.

I am glad that the Postmaster General has promised to further investigate the complaints of the people of Dickson, and I feel satisfied that the fads will justify him in establishing a post office there.

I wish to remind the Postmaster General that the town of North Toronto has applied for a free postal delivery. North Toronto has a population of nearly 5,000 ^ at present. Its southern boundary adjoins the northern boundary of the city of Toronto and its streets are in fact a continuation of the streets of the city. North Toronto has 16 miles of good sidewalk, and if the Postmaster General desires to accommodate the greatest number he should start with a town like North Toronto.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The streets of North Toronto are a continuation of the streets of Toronto?
Yes.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I may tell my hon friend (Mr. Wallace) that I have taken

note of the vernal representations he made to me the other day. The hon. gentleman from York (Mr. Maclean) has also made representations to me on the subject, and I am having inquiry made. Probably during the summer we will be able to provide for free letter delivery in that section of the city.
Post Office-Miscellaneous, $50,000.
Where is the post office now in the town of Holland? The office was burned there about two months ago. It was a rented building.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: ' We would, of course, rent another post office. If the postmaster was the proprietor, he would probably rebuild.

1 have been asked if a free rural mail delivery route could be established in a portion of the township of Innisfail. There is a thickly settled farming locality and a summer resort which would be served by a loop. There is no post office and no mail route there now, although in the summer a temporary office has been opened at the summer resort. Peninsular park.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: If my hon. friend will spend a quarter of an hour with me on Tuesday, we might see what can be done. I remember a request from that township for the establishment of a rural mail delivery. We might overcome the difficulty by establishing a post office at the summer resort.	,
Has the department received a request for a post office at Gow-ganda Junction?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Yes, we have aho an application from a company wishing to undertake the mail service.
A post office will be put there?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes.

There is an increase of $1,000 there.
Mr. FIELDING There is no special reason except the general enlargement of business.

speechtext: There has been a change of the words in that item.

speechtext:
The amendment is to strike out, 'to assist in the

speechtext:
It is intended to give them a little more elasticity in the application of the vote.
Miscellaneous-Grant to the Canadian Handicrafts Guild, $1,000.
What institution is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It is an association which is working amongst the people in the country parts to teach them home industries and give them samples to help them in their work.
Miscellaneous-To provide for expenses of Conservation Commission-further amount required, $35,000.
Is this the only amount granted for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was $15,000 in the main estimates.
That makes $50,000 altogether?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
Miscellaneous-Ottawa Branch of Royal Mint-further amount for Mint maintenance, $25,000.
I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if he has considered the advisability of coining nickel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend was not present when we had a good discussion the other day on the subject. There are some reasons in favour of the nickel and quite a number against it. The objection to nickel is that it is a white metal and, many people think, too easily confused with silver. However, the matter has not been determined. For the present we continue our old forms of currency in silver.
Might I suggest, we have done a very good day's work, and as we were up late last night, I think we should adjourn.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the suggestion is reasonable.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business for Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: First, the Combines Bill, and, if that is disposed of, the Insurance Bill.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Monday, April 25, 1910.
